Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.
Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.
Sponsorship update
It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.
SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.
The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction,
possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;
I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations.
Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search
because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos.
Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately?
I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from,
how many users I have, or what they’re up to.
At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet, but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.
On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,
you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.
I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key, I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key, and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to, and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again (ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good part of my career helping people streamline and automate).
C++ Index…?
Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.
I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go, in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement, but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax, and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.
Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms that already exists for on-heap structures but not off; bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow, it just chafes.
Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine, performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.
To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact, and if we do I doubt it will be massive, as the Java implementation is already very optimized, and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.
Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor for continuing this even if the performance doesn’t materialize.
I’m doing this quite slowly one component at a time, measuring twice and cutting once, finding good abstractions that lean into C++’s strengths rather than doing a straight translation. In part because this is supremely fiddly and technical work, and in part because there genuinely isn’t any rush and if there is much performance to gain it’s probably in staring at the problem long enough I find better alternative approaches. I did manage to lean more into lock-free algorithms in the buffer pool for example. Translation probably won’t be finished this year at this pace.
Many things are undecided: Haven’t decided on where to draw the interface boundary yet. Neither do I have a public git repo for this. May still scrap the entire idea as a silly boondoggle. We’ll just have to see where it goes.
On the off chance this rambling mess gets posted on a link aggregator somewhere, I anticipate two types of people will crawl out of the woodwork. I’ll address their concerns in advance.
“Why not Rust/Zig/Odin/${MY_HOBBY_HORSE_LANGUAGE}? C++ is not memory safe! Haven’t you heard that C++ is bad? Look at this diseased rat comic I found on /r/programming!”
My friend in Christ, I use C++ because I’m experienced with C++, and have built nontrivial stuff with in in the past, I’m familiar with the tooling and also kinda enjoy it. It can not be overstated how technical this code is, it’s more than hard enough in a language I’m familiar with, let alone one I’d have to learn as I go. I don’t need to do it blindfolded using a dance mat in a barrel going down the niagara falls for this to be difficult.
"${FRONTIER_MODEL} could one-shot this in less than ${TIME}!"
Probably true? The source is all pretty well tested, with a reference implementation to boot. Seems like very favorable circumstances for a competent coding model.
That said, even without turning over rocks such as “externalities of the datacenter buildout”, “externalities of AI training”, and “legal ownership status of AI-generated code”—I don’t think such angles of attack do much to convince anyone who isn’t already convinced—if AI did the translation I sure as heck couldn’t go on to then maintain that code[1][2].
Even in the best case, this is me at the edge of my programming abilities. Performance critical low level programming is hard enough to wrap your head around if you were the one who designed the code, let alone if it was vibe coded. I’d be on the hook for an AI subscription perpetually hoping and praying the token prices wouldn’t ever go up. This is a nonstarter for the same reasons the search engine runs on its own hardware and not in the cloud. You can’t be truly independent if you’re subject to the whims of a landlord.
From a project management perspective, I’m not rushing anything to market. Project still has years of runway. I’m not beholden to any investors to deliver profits. Even if I wanted to, I have no employees to replace other than my self. What I would trade away is the very immersion in the problem domain that’s allowed me to get as far as I have with this project. What I’m expecting to be getting out of it is improved developer ergonomics and maybe a bit of performance if the aforementioned problem-immersion-thing pans out. That’s not something that brings me money, and something I can do because the project is in a fairly stable and mature state.
Thus, regardless of what happens in the future with AI, there isn’t an obvious opportunity cost to holding off.
Heck, let’s just consider popular future predictions about AI, where does this leave me?
- AI bet pays of and models become exponentially more powerful, much cheaper, and ubiquitous like tap water: How shortsighted would it be to pay for crappy AI today when I could save my money and get exponentially better or more AI for the same dollars in the future? I’d have to really hate having money to do such a thing.
- OpenThropic IPOs, vocal shareholders from Ferenginar quite insistently ask where they money at, token prices go up singificantly: Only a problem if you’re dependent on AI.
- AI investment bubble crashes and it’s raining bankers like October 1929: Bad for everyone, but especially bad if you’re dependent on AI.
- Tech prists in SV chant binharic hymns as the Machine God emerges and the chosen of humanity transcends into the cyber rapture: Kind of orthogonal to whether I build this index port by hand.
- Zoomers decide that Kazcinski was right all along and instigate a Butlerian Jihad: Mostly a problem if you’re dependent on AI.
- Rise of the Machines, hydraulic press youtube channel stomping on a human face forever: Inconvenient regardless of choice of action.
[1] Lesser minds would think models outputting unmanitainable code is a sign of the superiority of AI. I’ll refer you to the most problematic prophet, Terry Davis, for that one.
[2] I used an m-dash aside in that paragraph. Anyone reckon mr robot wrote this? Discuss in groups.

US Spy Agencies Suffer Breach of Some Unclassified Information (nytimes.com) 2
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to U.S. officials and other people familiar with the matter. The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the people familiar with the issues said. It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people.
Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data. Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments. It is not uncommon for federal agencies to suffer cybersecurity breaches, but several have recently detected intrusions into some of their systems, prompting heightened concern among current and former U.S. intelligence officials. When asked about the recent hack of the FBI crime database, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said breaches occurred frequently and that there was no cause for alarm. "Cyberprobing, cyberincidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time."
"And what we're hearing about the F.B.I., and what I've talked to them about is, they have an incident. They're dealing with it in the ordinary course."

Serving Qwen via AWS Lambdas for fun and 80x negative profit
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-25
04:28:06 CET
12:28:06 KST

Serving Qwen via 5,600 Lambdas for fun and 80x negative profit
Who needs a GPU?
In my work at Bevyl I was really impressed by the performance and cost characteristics of AWS Lambdas. They can massively distribute and fan out CPU-bound work, which is amazing for things like ffmpeg on long videos.
So I was curious if it was possible to run inference on self-hosted models using Lambdas. It was a random idea built on a hunch, and I like to prove such ideas right or wrong by building. In this case I was very wrong, but it was a good lesson!
I picked H2O-Lightning, a fine-tune of Qwen3.5-4B, because I wanted a small model built for decisions. I figured if this architecture had any legs, only doing decision models (a single forward pass) is the move. A decision model reads a document and answers a question about it by picking one option.
Fanning out
So the trick, if it's possible, would be fanning out. I was inspired how Remotion uses massively parallelized Lambdas to render videos.
I wanted to prove this was possible to do, so I kept a constraint of a 3 GB limit for Lambdas. The whole model is 9.3 GB, so it does not fit in one. But it has 32 layers of about 225 MB each, and one layer fits. That gave me one Lambda job per layer per block of tokens.
Think of the Lambda as a simple idempotent API. A job reads inputs from S3, does the math, and writes one object back.
x = load(f"{doc}/{layer - 1}/{block}")
memory = load(f"{doc}/{layer}/{block - 1}")
y, memory = model.layers[layer](x, memory)
s3.put_object(
    Key=f"{doc}/{layer}/{block}",
    Body=pack(y, memory),
)
Each job waits on the layer above for the same block and on its own previous block. Each layer starts one step after the layer above it, like a staircase 32 layers deep.
I'm proud of the win: splitting a model call across 5,600 Lambdas is kinda wild.
The bill
If it was 40x slower but 50% cheaper, that'd be interesting.
Reading a 4,000-token document takes 17 seconds and costs 3.4 cents. That works out to $8.40 per million tokens. Google sells a hosted decision model, Gemini Decision 1, for $0.10 per million tokens, so the same read costs 0.04 cents there. Mine is more than 80 times more expensive.
Takeaways
Model engineering is not so hard in 2026!
I'm a dumb application developer, but I was able to play with model layers and transformers API pretty easily! With good devex, it feels like open models are just another API at this point.
I need a GPU
Learned this the hard way but a very powerful lesson! One layer over a few thousand tokens is a big matrix multiply, which is what GPUs are built for. My goal was to learn anyway so it's a good lesson.
Freedom ain't free
CPU still costs dollars, there's no arbitrage here.

Show HN: Sliding-panes React UI library (inspired by WebOS Enyo)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-25
03:10:18 UTC
12:10:18 KST

Sashay
Drag the edge between two panes to resize them. The edge settles at a simple fraction of the width, and a pane with no room left slides under its neighbour. The layout can be saved in the URL.
Why panes?
Power users want to arrange their screen the way they work. Panes give them that without making the interface complicated: each pane is an ordinary view, and the only new control is the edge between them.
That makes them a good middle ground between a fully customisable UI, where any panel can go anywhere, and a simple responsive layout that decides everything for you.
Hang it in a frame.
// @vcarl/sashay/react
<Sashay
  onLayoutChange={save}>
  <Pane id="list"
    title="List"
    focus={1/3}>…</Pane>
  <Pane id="detail"
    title="Detail"
    focus={1/2}>…</Pane>
</Sashay>
Snaps to simple fractions.
Dividers rest on fractions with a denominator up to six, so a layout saved on a laptop still makes sense on a monitor. The grid gets finer as the frame gets wider.
Guide: Your first frame →
Throw it.
A quick throw carries the divider one or two snaps past where you let go. Release speed is read from the last 90 ms, so a slow drag still lands exactly where you put it.
Guide: Your first frame →
A bar for each pane.
Any pane can have a bar at its bottom for filters, settings or a table of contents. It expands over the pane and works the same on a phone.
Guide: Bottom bars →
Deep stacks fold into a spine.
Drill down as far as you like. Panes that no longer fit fold into a slim spine, with a tab for each. Drag cost stays flat at a thousand deep.
Guide: Navigation stacks →
Deep linked pane arrangements
Which panes are open, how wide they are, and which bars are open all fit in a short code you can keep in the URL. Share the link and the other person sees the same arrangement.
Guide: Layout in the URL →

Macrohistory in Six Facts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-25
03:04:46 UTC
12:04:46 KST

Joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models. Economists often seem to forget that some of the most important theories in physics are either verified or refuted by a single observation, or a limited number of observations (e.g. Einstein’s theory of relativity, or the theory of black holes).”
Can we condense down the most important lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts? Here is one attempt: macrohistory in six (plus or minus) facts.
What I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences. On the Y-axis is life satisfaction, based on going around and asking people, ‘on a scale of zero to ten, how satisfied are you with your life’.
In richer countries, on average people are happier.
Or – in richer countries, on average people live longer:
Or – in richer countries, fewer babies die:
Are all these good things just coming from people working more? No – in richer countries, people work less; and as countries become richer over time, people work less:
More intangible things, too. You can ask people how much they trust their neighbors. In richer countries, people trust their neighbors more:
Of course, we know market capitalism has its flaws – for example, richer countries emit more CO2 per person:
And all of this is correlation not causation.
But we’re going to run with this, and use GDP per person as our measure of how well we are doing.
Which brings us to:
This is the most important fact about human history.
We are ∼10 times richer than our great-great-great grandparents, who themselves in turn were ∼2 times as rich as Jesus of Nazareth.
Everyone used to be poor. This is the most important fact about macro history.
Why did we used to be poor? We lived in a Malthusian hellscape:
This shows the real wage of workers in England since 1250.
Prior to the Industrial Revolution, any time wages rose, more babies would survive to adulthood, parents would have more babies, and the population would rise until wages were driven back to subsistence.
We lived in a Malthusian hellscape. Until:
The Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in human history.
We went from 0.01% growth per year, up to 0.1% with the Industrial Revolution around 1750, to 1% with the Second Industrial Revolution around 1870, to the modern 2% growth rate.
The Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in macro history. It also brought about:
The growth explosion from the Industrial Revolution did not take place everywhere and all at once. Many countries did not see faster growth and rising GDP per person until much later – and many still have not seen these much at all.
But let’s talk first about the frontier.
This is the most important fact in modern macro. Growth at the technological frontier – measured here as GDP per person in the United States – has been a shockingly steady 2% per year for the last 150 years.
You can see a temporary blip down for the Great Depression, but otherwise the trend has been remarkably constant.
Running water, electricity, automobiles, computers, the web – all show up here as a continuation of a steady 2% per year trend.
What about the rest of the world?
The figure here has on the X-axis, income per person per day. You can see, for example, that even the poorest 11% of people in the United States have on average a higher income than the median person in Bangladesh or Ethiopia.
Income varies enormously across countries. Those of us born in the United States are so, so lucky.
Well, are we stuck with these enormous differences? No:
Here again we see the United States up top as the frontier.
Japan and South Korea, at the turn of the 20th century, were ∼as poor as sub-Saharan Africa is today. But Japan and South Korea caught up close to the United States. There are growth miracles.
But there are also growth disasters. Argentina at the turn of the 20th century was one of the richest countries in the world. But it has stagnated, relative to the frontier. A classic basket case.
And there are countries like Nigeria, which have never experienced much sustained growth at all.
What should we expect of the future? This takes us to the most fun fact, the most speculative:
Over the long sweep of history, aggregate GDP growth is speeding up.
What I have plotted here is how long it takes for world GDP to double. This goes back to 1 million years ago. Measuring GDP in 1 million BC is hard, but for our purposes I feel good about these numbers.
We’ve gone from doubling every 100,000 years down to a modern doubling time of every 35 or so years.
———
Now, to the natural question: what should we expect about growth in the future?
I think it really comes down to: which prior do you want to anchor to?
Do you want to anchor to the last 150 years or so, with our constant 2% growth and doubling every 35 years?
Or do you want to anchor to the long sweep of macrohistory, where growth has been speeding up?
We live in a weird time.
Walking around outside, I think we should really feel bombarded with this fact, every day. All these buildings? All these people? All this stuff?
This is all kind of crazy. It’s all a little bonkers. Compared to the grand sweep of macrohistory, we live in a weird time.
I found these “Six Big Facts of Macrohistory” particularly useful as framing when teaching my undergrad macro course for the first time last fall: teaching GDP construction (fact 0), the Malthusian model (fact 1), the theories of the Industrial Revolution (fact 2), the Solow model (facts 3-5), and the endogenous growth model (fact 6).
It was pedagogically very useful to have this catechism of the Six Facts to review at the start of many classes, to anchor the students to where we were in the course.
It was also useful for me, for setting a target for the bare minimum that students might remember in a decade. Do I expect them to remember the capital accumulation equation of the Solow model? No. Or even the idea of income vs. substitution effects? For the vast majority – no, not really.
Can I hope that they pick up a gut-level sense, in their bones, that everyone used to be poor? That’s an extremely important idea, a realistic goal, and yet an idea that the vast majority of people do not know or have not properly internalized.
I also think the Six Big Facts of Macrohistory is a useful attempt to condense “what should any well-informed civilian know about macro and macrohistory”. E.g. my microeconomist wife, or my parents.
What are the runner-up facts not listed here? Structural transformation and urbanization? The demographic transition? Women’s emancipation or rising health would be the natural top candidates, but are captured (if perhaps buried) in Fact 0.
Again, underlying these figures is the astounding work of generations of economic historians, demographers, national statistical agencies, and others.

Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-25
03:04:37 UTC
12:04:37 KST

Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.
More recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.
Why the iOS Safari Experience Sucks
What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.
How can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.
Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.
High Refresh Rate Interactions
Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.
If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.
In order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.
- Want a 1:1 trackpad experience? We just measure only when the finger is pressed.
- Want a true trackball with native momentum? We just make it an infinitely scrollable region.
- Want native bounce? We configure over-scroll padding and set the bounds of the container.
- Want a dial with notches? Snap points!
The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.
Creating “The Controller”
I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.
Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.
First, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.
Next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.
What finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.
Each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.
Safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering update queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty requestAnimationFrame loop is all we need to do that.
This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.
I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.
Squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.
Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.
If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive touchmove listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.
Just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.
One issue remains. scrollTop and scrollLeft are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.
If you want to use the viewport itself as a controller, you can choose to invasively set the initial-scale in the same way, but this comes with some caveats. You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.
From here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.
Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.
Breaking the 60 FPS Render Barrier
Now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.
The vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?
Ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own bug tracker is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.
Asking Google yields the following preamble.
There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 <canvas> (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.
Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.
Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering update. Low Power Mode throttles further.
Well, as of today… you can!
At first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.
Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.
In WebKit on iOS, if we create a canvas element and call transferControlToOffscreen, we get an OffscreenCanvas back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an OffscreenCanvas pushes a frame.
Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.
Jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.
Putting it All Together
Now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of Ando’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.
Applying Our Learnings
This page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.
When the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.
As the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter how the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.
On this page, components using requestAnimationFrame for illustrative reasons update the texture from the main thread. Components using OffscreenCanvas post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.
After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.
Building a Tab Bar Component
Building the Structure
Let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.
Layout of Controllers
We’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.
Building the State Machine
We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the new events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.
- If a controller is being touched we then magnify & lift the lens.
- We know where to move the lens based on the controller’s offset since the touch began.
- If the user pulls past the bounds of the tab bar, we stretch the bar towards their finger.
- Depending on the offset, when the user stops touching the controller, we settle the lens on the nearest tab.
Adding razzle-dazzle
Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.
Performance
I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.
Over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.
Wrapping Up
Liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!
Disclaimers
Would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make OffscreenCanvas’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after Lochie Axon unveiled the web-haptics library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

Lua for Data Representation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-25
03:04:12 UTC
12:04:12 KST

lua for data representation
my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.
lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]]. however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]). the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===], not with a ]] or a ]==], or a ]====].
here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:
local function stringize(str)
    local equal_signs = ""
    for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do
        if #e >= #equal_signs then
            equal_signs = e .. "="
        end
    end
    return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs)
end
of course, you can just use string.format with %q, but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.
anyway, download this file. if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.
design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.
styles of data representation
JSON style (LON?)
chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program.
return {
    foo = "bar",
    list = {1, 2, 3},
    rule_of_thirds = true,
}
if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead.
return (function() arbitrary_code() end)()
trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead.
INI style
what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.
you can have a file like this:
-- config.lua
foo = "bar"
list = {1, 2, 3}
rule_of_thirds = true
then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this:
local config = {}
assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))()
imperative style
lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.
path "/path/to/things"
config {
    foo = "bar",
    list = {1, 2, 3},
    rule_of_thirds = true,
}
lipsum [[
    Voluptatibus laudantium et omnis ut debitis. Similique omnis molestias
    consequuntur. Praesentium corporis omnis nihil et quidem dolore. Veritatis
    fugiat eaque corporis eligendi officiis praesentium. Libero quo vero
    temporibus impedit sit inventore assumenda
]]
programming in lua provides a real world example of this.
security considerations
the major problem with using an entire programming language to represent data is that untrusted data can be readily crafted to be malicious. indeed, I would not use this technique for untrusted data. with that in mind, it is possible to solve or mitigate the potential vulnerabilities.
the main technique for sandboxing lua is controlling the environment. when using lua for data representation, an empty enivronment is the most appropriate (or, an environment that only exposes data constructors). this prevents any I/O or access to the larger program’s state. preventing access to all standard library functions is safest. there are a few standard library functions that have consequences you might not expect.
another concern is denial of service. this is trickier to prevent. it’s fairly trivial to construct a lua chunk which does not return (while true do end). debug.sethook can mitigate this somewhat. even so, it’s probably possible to construct something that uses excessive amounts of memory. that said, denial of service is significantly less problematic than the vulnerabilities that are completely avoided by depriving the untrusted code of any standard library functions.
finally, make sure to reject lua bytecode. untrusted lua bytecode is not safe and may cause arbitrary nasal demons in the lua interpreter. load can accept both bytecode and lua source by default. however, passing "t" for the mode parameter prevents this.
why?
clearly, it’s silly to bring in the entire lua interpreter where you would just use JSON or INI. where this use case of lua shines is when you’re already using lua for a project (and then you already have this powerful data description language), or when you need something with a lot of power or flexibility.
these mini languages can be extended to arbitrary complexity and nuance. unlike JSON, you can add arbitrary type constructors, or anything at all. you can build any kind of language you want, and that’s how lua is designed to be used, and it’s actually approximately the story of how it was invented.
if you’re anything like me, this will sound a little familiar. indeed, many have said similar things about lisp and forth. both of those languages have very different approaches but reach the same conclusion of “inventing your own language”. I believe lua belongs in their pantheon.
bonus content
python? js? ruby? what the hell are those? all I care about is LUA.

I've been drinking wine in my kitchen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-25
03:02:10 UTC
12:02:10 KST

I’ve been drinking wine in my kitchen
See I don’t even like alcohol much. Like, I’ll have a half-glass of wine at a fancy dinner if everyone else is having some, or one beer at a reception, but that’s it. These days, though, can you blame me?
Yesterday, as you all probably saw, hot on the heels of its proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, Anthropic released a proof of Valiant’s VP≠VNP conjecture—a central algebraic analogue of the P≠NP conjecture, and considered a “warmup” to proving P≠NP since the late 1970s. Then, later the same day, OpenAI released a proof of the VP≠VNP conjecture as well.
You can read all about the VP vs. VNP problem in Section 6.5 of my P vs. NP survey. But briefly, for those tuning in from home, Valiant’s conjecture says that the permanent of an n×n matrix has no algebraic circuits (that is, circuits built out of addition and multiplication gates and constants) of size polynomial in n, unlike the determinant, which does. Anthropic’s result says that a circuit of size exp(Ω(log4/3 n)) is needed, whereas OpenAI gets exp(Ω(log5/4 n)): so, more than polynomial albeit less than exponential. As is often the case, the best known upper bound here is ~2n. The lower bounds are said to work over all fields of characteristic other than 2. (What’s special about 2? Over a field of characteristic 2, addition and subtraction are the same, so the permanent just is the determinant, and is easy to compute!)
From what little I understand so far, the proof techniques in the Anthropic and OpenAI papers look similar. They both do some sort of highly nontrivial “compression” or “shortening,” followed in the end by a diagonalization—the oldest trick in the book! Diagonalization is what should let these arguments evade the infamous natural proofs barrier. There’s probably also a story to tell about how the arguments evade an algebraic-circuit version of the relativization barrier, but I don’t know how to tell it yet.
One immediate implication of these results is that, if you want to map an n×n matrix A to an m×m matrix B whose entries are affine functions of the entries of A, and have the permanent of A be equal to the determinant of B, then m must be exp(Ω(log4/3 n)). This was the question directly targeted by Ketan Mulmuley’s Geometric Complexity Theory program—which, however, these papers don’t use, taking a more direct route to the desired lower bound.
As is de rigeur these days, the proofs come with Lean, formally certifying their correctness to a level considerably beyond what we’d normally demand for a math paper published in a journal. If recent experience is any guide, this will not prevent boatloads of morons from denying that AI could possibly have solved these problems, and latching onto anything whatsoever (e.g., unused Lean code or Lean that deviates slightly from the natural-language version) to declare the proofs to be fallacious … and such claims will then go viral, lapped up by an eager audience on Bluesky and other places hungry for AI denial. If there’s any real technical issue with the proofs, I’ll be happy to hear about it from experts, but my patience for arguing with the flat-earthers is at an end.
Daniel Harlow asked me whether the proof of VP≠VNP raises my confidence in P≠NP itself, which I’d lowered from 97% to 95% in light of OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s recent refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis. I said sure, I’m now back up to 96%.
The possibility that this will be followed up soon by a proof of P≠NP itself has not escaped my notice, or anyone else’s, certainly not at the AI companies. Will the big one come tomorrow? Next week? Next month? In a year? Who the hell knows? Hence the wine drinking, which I wouldn’t call sad, but just … thirsty.
If that wasn’t enough for you—if you still want more—yesterday Sanjeev Khanna, Aaron Putterman, and Junkai Song posted an ECCC preprint with a deterministic linear-time algorithm for finding minimum spanning trees in graphs. (The best previously-known algorithm was ridiculously close to linear time—n α(n) where α is the inverse of the Ackermann function—but not quite. A randomized linear-time algorithm was known.) This was a huge open problem for decades, and one that my wife Dana spent roughly two years working on.
Khanna et al. write, “the main ideas in [our] paper were entirely generated by AI—specifically 6.2 Astra, on a mixture of Ultra and Max effort—with minimal human intellectual intervention. The authors then worked to first carefully verify, and then to simplify and clarify the treatment.”
Anyway, yeah, tonight I’ll again raise my glass, I’ll pray that at the bottom of this terrifying rollercoaster lies a world that my children and I will be glad to inhabit, and I’ll mutter to myself the eternal words:
God would like us to be joyful
Even though our hearts lie panting on the floor;
How much more can we be joyful,
When there’s really something
To be joyful for.
To life, to life, l’chaim!
L’chaim, l’chaim, to life!
It gives you something to think about,
Something to drink about,
Drink l’chaim, to life!
Update: See Lance’s post for more.

The ProofAtlas ranking
Top 500 open problems in mathematics
ranked by LLM-assessed importance
Explore questions in mathematics, computation, and mathematical physics, with exact statements, status notes, and sources.
This is a model-based assessment of mathematical importance, not an expert consensus or a forecast of which problems will be solved next.
Resolved problems from earlier editions remain available with their original ranks and sources.
2 entries have conditional ranks. Each entry explains why.
How the ranking works
What importance means here. Each entry is a specific mathematical question. Importance considers the significance of a resolution, centrality within its field, reach across fields, scholarly and historical fame, broader recognition, and scientific or practical impact.
How problems are ranked. LLMs compare pairs of problems. A reliability-weighted model combines those judgments into the ranking, with calibration across model families. The model-family weights are OpenAI 1.00, Claude 1.00, GLM 0.95, and DeepSeek 0.90. These are modeling choices, not measured probabilities of correctness.
What a rank means. Nearby ranks can be uncertain. The expanded entries include available ranking ranges and comparison counts. Filtering or alphabetizing the directory preserves every problem’s rank in this edition.
Diagnostics from the preceding source fit. After the reported resolutions, edition ranks were compacted without a new numerical fit. The displayed uncertainty ranges and comparison counts come from the preceding fit of 1,280 targets; the current eligible pool contains 1,122. These diagnostics were not recomputed for the smaller pool.
Related and nested problems. A substantial subproblem or generalization may receive its own rank when it has independent mathematical standing. Families identify narrow groups of related questions; an implication alone does not merge their families. The ranking process checks family crowding, including a diagnostic retaining the highest-ranked member of each family. Family membership does not itself change scores, impose a quota, or create an automatic penalty.
Dates and sources. The edition date identifies this list. A status review date, when recorded, appears separately inside each entry; it does not promise that the literature has been checked since then. Source links identify the exact formulation and available status evidence.
The ranking preserves a fixed edition. Separately dated status notes cover 176 of 500 entries; this is not a fresh literature review of the whole list. Recent resolution claims and formulation concerns are marked below with their historical ranks retained.
Find an open problem
Select a problem to read its exact statement, why it matters, status, sources, and related research.
Families are ordered by their highest-ranked member in the complete edition. Families have no importance score; every problem keeps its edition rank. Filters show matching members within that fixed family order.

- Rank013NP versus P/polyCan every yes-or-no problem with short, efficiently checkable evidence for yes answers be solved by Boolean circuits of polynomial size, if a separate circuit may be chosen for each input length? No efficient method of constructing those circuits is required.Theoretical computer science Exact statement Determine the truth of NP subseteq P/poly. Here NP consists of languages over finite binary strings accepted by nondeterministic Turing machines in polynomial time. P/poly consists of languages L for which there exist constants C>=1 and integer k>=1 and Boolean circuits C_n for all n>=0, of size at most C(n+1)^k, deciding membership in L on every length-n input. Circuits are finite acyclic single-output circuits with fan-in-two AND/OR, fan-in-one NOT, input bits and hardwired constants0/1; count all nodes. Each language has its own bound and circuit family, with no uniform generation requirement. Why it matters Containment would collapse the polynomial hierarchy to its second level by the Karp–Lipton theorem. Noncontainment would establish a general circuit-size barrier for an NP language and imply P ≠ NP. Status Open NP containment in nonuniform P/poly remains open; February 2026 notes pose the matching general-circuit question. Restricted circuits and Karp–Lipton implications do not decide it. Status reviewed Sources

- Rank016BQP Versus NP: Complete Language-Class RelationHow do efficient quantum solving and efficient classical verification compare for yes-or-no problems? - Rank074Weight–Monodromy ConjectureMonodromy organizes a variety’s l-adic cohomology into layers. Are the Frobenius eigenvalues on each layer algebraic, with the absolute sizes predicted by its degree and layer index in every complex embedding, for every smooth proper variety over a nonarchimedean local field and every prime l different from the residue characteristic?Number theory & arithmetic geometry Exact statement Let K be ANY nonarchimedean local field with finite residue field F_q of characteristic p, X ANY proper smooth variety over K, i>=0, and l ANY prime different from p. Put V=H^i_et(X_over_Kbar,Qbar_l), retaining the original K. On an open inertia subgroup the action is unipotent and defines nilpotent monodromy N:V->V(-1), with its Galois-equivariant Tate twist. Let M be the unique increasing monodromy filtration centred at zero: N(M_j) is contained in M_(j-2)(-1), and N^a:gr^M_a(V)->gr^M_(-a)(V)(-a) is an isomorphism for every a>=0. For EVERY integer j and ANY lift Phi of geometric Frobenius of F_q, every eigenvalue alpha on gr^M_j(V) is conjectured to be algebraic and have absolute value q^((i+j)/2) under ALL complex embeddings. This is purity of weight i+j. Defining N on an open inertia subgroup does not replace K or q. Finite-extension proof reductions must change cardinality and Frobenius consistently. Extending l-adic coefficients does not change the target. The equivalent source convention compares zero-centred M_j with W_(i+j); weight-filtration existence is not an added unresolved assertion. No restriction to projective, semistable, geometrically connected or special complete-intersection varieties is imposed. l=p, crystalline, torsion and arbitrary rigid-analytic analogues are not substituted. Why it matters A proof would force every such eigenvalue to have absolute value q^((i + j)/2) under every complex embedding. It would link local monodromy to prescribed Frobenius weights without imposing projectivity or semistability. Status Open · subcases solved Weight–monodromy remains open, with solved subcases. Complete intersections in abelian varieties are a subcase, and 2026 formality work assumes weight–monodromy. Rigid-analytic counterexamples or l=p analogues are not the stated smooth proper algebraic l != p statement. Status reviewed Sources

- Rank085PSPACE versus EXPTIMEIf a deterministic algorithm solves a yes-or-no problem in time 2^(n^k) for some fixed k, must another deterministic algorithm solve it using only polynomially many working-memory bits in the input length n?Theoretical computer science Exact statement Determine whether PSPACE=EXPTIME for languages over finite binary strings in the standard deterministic multitape Turing-machine model with a read-only input tape and work tapes. PSPACE is the union over integers k>=1 of DSPACE(n^k), with asymptotic constant factors allowed and read-only input cells not counted as work space. EXPTIME is the union over integers k>=1 of DTIME(2^(n^k)), with asymptotic constant factors allowed. Machines are total deciders that halt on every input. This is an unrelativized equality of the full classes, not of one fixed resource exponent. Why it matters An equality would show that polynomial memory suffices for every computation in the full exponential-time class. A separation would identify a decision problem whose time bound can be exponential but whose memory requirements exceed every polynomial. Status Open PSPACE versus EXPTIME remains open with bounded recency evidence. The Czerwinski separation was withdrawn in March 2024 with an independent critique, which defeats that claim but does not certify absence of every later one. Status reviewed Sources

- Rank140Congruent Number ProblemExactly which positive integers occur as the area of a right triangle whose three side lengths are rational numbers?Number theory & arithmetic geometryElliptic curve ranks and congruent numbers · 3 problems Exact statement Determine exactly which positive integers are congruent numbers, i.e. areas of right triangles with all three sides rational, equivalently for which squarefree n the elliptic curve y^2 = x^3 - n^2 x has a rational point with y != 0. Why it matters A complete answer would classify these rational triangles by their integer areas. For squarefree n, it would also determine exactly when y² = x³ − n²x has a rational point with nonzero y. Status Open · subcases solved October 7, 2026: OpenAI’s October 6 release reports partial progress. The rank-equality theorem applies in particular to congruent-number curves y^2=x^3-n^2 x when a full q-power Selmer group has corank at most one; it then identifies whether their Mordell-Weil rank is zero or one. There is no unconditional classification of every squarefree n or a guarantee that every congruent-number curve meets the low-corank hypothesis. Congruent-number curves have rational two-torsion, so the companion identifies their actual rank when their full 2-power Selmer corank is zero or one. This does not decide congruence for every squarefree n: higher-corank twists and an exhaustive criterion are not covered. The low-corank 2-converse applies to those quadratic twists of y^2=x^3-x whose full 2-power Selmer corank is zero or one, giving the corresponding actual rank. Analytic densities and a mean over signed squarefree twists do not by themselves classify every individual positive congruent number. No independent proof audit or Lean verification was performed for this update. Status reviewed Sources

- Rank150Voevodsky's Smash-Nilpotence ConjectureIf an algebraic cycle with rational coefficients has zero intersection number against every complementary cycle, must multiplying copies of it on a product of sufficiently many copies of the variety make it zero modulo rational equivalence, for every smooth projective variety over any field?Number theory & arithmetic geometry Exact statement For every field k, every smooth projective k-variety X of dimension d, every integer 0<=r<=d, and every class alpha in CH^r(X)_Q (codimension-r cycles modulo rational equivalence with rational coefficients), assume deg(alpha.beta)=0 for every beta in CH^(d-r)(X)_Q. Voevodsky's smash-nilpotence assertion is that there exists an integer N>=1, depending on alpha, for which the N-fold EXTERNAL product alpha times ... times alpha is zero in CH^(Nr)(X^N)_Q, where X^N is the fibre product over k. No algebraic-closure, characteristic-zero or geometric-connectedness hypothesis is imposed; disconnected smooth projective schemes are interpreted on their pure-dimensional components. The reverse implication, smash-nilpotent implies numerically trivial, is known, so this is equality of numerical and smash equivalence for rational cycles. Neither intersection powers on X, composition powers of correspondences, integral coefficients, nor a uniform or computable exponent replaces this assertion. Why it matters A proof would characterize numerical triviality by actual vanishing after enough external products. The required exponent may depend on the cycle, and the products take place on powers of the variety rather than within the original variety. - Historical rank022Hilbert's Tenth Problem over the RationalsIs there an algorithm that always halts and correctly decides whether any given integer-coefficient polynomial, in any finite number of variables, has a rational solution?Logic, foundations & set theorySource-reported disproved Historical rank #22 in the Oct 6, 2026 edition. This entry is outside the current open ranking. Exact statement covered by this update There exists a total algorithm which, given any finite encoding of a multivariate polynomial f in Z[x_1,...,x_n] with arbitrary finite n and integer coefficients, halts and correctly decides whether there is q in Q^n with f(q)=0. Standard computably interconvertible polynomial encodings are equivalent; no uniform running-time complexity bound is part of the assertion. Status update Source-reported disproved Resolved (disproved) on the basis of the OpenAI mathematics release of 6 October 2026. Exact scope reviewed; proofs not independently audited, refereeing not independently confirmed, and Lean artifacts not executed. Family 004: The target is the existence of a total decision algorithm for arbitrary finite-variable integer-coefficient polynomials having rational zeros. The principal abstract denies precisely that algorithm, explicitly making the number of variables part of the input. Its negative answer disproves the target assertion without changing coefficient field, solution field, or input arity. Status reviewed Resolution sources Earlier ranking context A positive answer would supply a universal decision procedure for rational solvability, with no efficiency guarantee. A negative answer would establish that no algorithm can settle every polynomial input while always terminating. Earlier status note Open Hilbert's tenth problem over Q remains open. Results for finitely generated rings or languages with extra height predicates do not give a decision/undecidability result for ordinary rational Diophantine solvability. Recorded . This note predates the resolution reported above. Earlier statement and context sources

- Historical rank029Unique Games ConjectureIn a graph-labeling game, each edge requires the two labels to match through a one-to-one rule. Is distinguishing games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where only a tiny fraction can be satisfied NP-hard, however small these two error thresholds are, with a fixed label set chosen for each pair of thresholds?Theoretical computer scienceSource-reported proved Historical rank #29 in the Oct 6, 2026 edition. This entry is outside the current open ranking. Exact statement covered by this update For every fixed pair of real constants epsilon, delta > 0 with epsilon + delta < 1, there exists an integer k >= 2, depending only on epsilon and delta, such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. An instance is a finite directed constraint graph G=(V,E) with E nonempty and, for each edge e=(v,w), a permutation pi_e of [k]. For a labeling L:V->[k], an edge is satisfied if pi_e(L(v))=L(w); val(G) is the largest fraction of satisfied edges over all labelings. Distinguish val(G) >= 1-epsilon from val(G) <= delta, with no requirement on instances between these thresholds. The graph is the growing input; epsilon, delta and k are fixed constants. NP-hardness means that every language in NP has such a reduction mapping yes inputs to the first promised set and no inputs to the second. Status update Source-reported proved Resolved (proved) on the basis of the OpenAI mathematics release of 6 October 2026. Exact scope reviewed; proofs not independently audited, refereeing not independently confirmed, and Lean artifacts not executed. Family 102: The manuscript asserts deterministic polynomial-time reductions from 3SAT to fixed-alphabet Unique Games with completeness 1-epsilon and soundness delta for every fixed epsilon,delta in (0,1/2). This covers the ranked range epsilon,delta>0, epsilon+delta<1: choose smaller positive parameters below 1/2 and below the requested values, giving stronger completeness and soundness promises. The alphabet remains fixed independently of the graph input. This is the ordinary UGC target, not merely a conditional approximation consequence. Status reviewed Resolution sources Earlier ranking context A proof would establish this hardness gap and support approximation thresholds obtained through Unique Games reductions. Claims of efficient-algorithm impossibility from NP-hardness would still require the assumption P ≠ NP. Earlier status note Open Classical UGC remains open. The accessible Hallelujah preprint's graphwise ratio strictly below 2 does not give the fixed uniform 2-epsilon improvement needed for its claimed contradiction. The linked journal full text was inaccessible; independent acceptance of a full disproof was not established. Recorded . This note predates the resolution reported above. Earlier statement and context sources

- Historical rank038Higher-dimensional Euclidean Kakeya conjectureIn four or more dimensions, must a compact set containing a unit line segment in every direction have full Hausdorff dimension? This asks for full fractal dimension, even when the set need not have positive volume.Analysis & PDESource-reported proved Historical rank #38 in the Oct 7, 2026 edition. This entry is outside the current open ranking. Exact statement covered by this update Prove or disprove that for every integer n >= 4, every compact set E in R^n that contains a unit line segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension n. Status update Source-reported proved OpenAI announcement of October 26, 2026. Corollary 9.1 asserts full Hausdorff dimension for every Euclidean Kakeya set in every dimension n>=2. This covers the exact ranked compact-set target for every n>=4. Status follows the existing OpenAI-release source-acceptance policy. Exact statement coverage was reviewed; proof correctness, refereeing and Lean execution were not independently verified. Status reviewed Resolution sources Earlier ranking context A proof would show that accommodating all directions forces full Hausdorff dimension in these spaces. A counterexample would contain every required segment within a compact set of smaller dimension. Earlier status note Open · subcases solved Earlier note (2026-09-14): The stated higher-dimensional Euclidean Kakeya target (n >= 4) remains open, with solved subcases. The solved three-dimensional theorem is outside that range. A February positive-volume preprint is unaccepted and does not overcome the arbitrary zero-measure Kakeya-set issue; September lifting results remain conditional. October 7, 2026: OpenAI’s October 6 release reports partial progress. The full Kakeya target requires full Hausdorff dimension in every dimension n at least four. The second manuscript proves precisely the n=4 subcase, even for noncompact and nonregular sets; dimensions n at least five remain outside the family. The separate three-dimensional maximal estimate does not turn this into an all-dimensional theorem. No independent proof audit or Lean verification was performed for this update. Recorded . Family 142: Theorem 1.1 supplies uniform deterministic complete factorization over F_p, including multiplicities, in polynomial bit complexity in degree and log p, without randomness, an integer-factorization or primitive-root oracle, or GRH. The standard prime-field reduction transfers this to F_q with q=p^m in the explicitly represented finite-field model stated in Section 2. For a squarefree f, form A=F_q[x]/(f) as an F_p algebra and compute the kernel B of a->a^p-a by F_p linear algebra. If f has r irreducible factors, B is F_p^r. For each basis element b of B, compute its minimal polynomial over F_p and factor that polynomial using Theorem 1.1; it splits into linear factors. The gcds of b-a with current factors of f, for those roots a in F_p, separate all components as the basis is exhausted. Every space and polynomial involved has dimension or degree at most m deg(f), and only polynomially many operations/calls are required. Since m log p=log q, the overhead remains polynomial in degree and log q. Usual deterministic squarefree decomposition, with finite-field pth-root extraction when needed, restores multiplicities. Family 199: The Tachikawa companion defines infinite dominant dimension as projectivity of every term in the regular left module's minimal injective resolution. Corollary 1.2 constructs Gamma_K=End_{A_K}(A_K direct-sum M_K)^op and states that it is a finite-dimensional K-algebra whose every minimal-injective-resolution term is projective but whose self-injective dimension is infinite. Finite-dimensional algebras over fields are Artin algebras; infinite self-injective dimension excludes self-injectivity, which would have injective dimension zero. Hence this is precisely a counterexample to the ranked implication, with the left-module convention made explicit by the opposite algebra. Characteristic two and the transcendental base field do not narrow the universal Artin-algebra target: one permitted counterexample suffices. Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of 'Perfect Resilience'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-25
03:00:39 UTC
12:00:39 KST

Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
Introduction
One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.
Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.
If a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.
Now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They showed that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.
“It’s a very elegant contribution,” said Michael Schapira, a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”
Think Globally, Act Locally
Imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?
One simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.
In principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.
This restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.
In a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each new packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.
With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” said Brighten Godfrey, a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.
Godfrey, Schapira, and their colleagues showed that in this model, perfect resilience isn’t always achievable. They did so by finding a single example of a network layout that can’t be made perfectly resilient. No matter what set of routing rules you choose, there’s always a pattern of link failures that will cause some packets to get stuck in a loop.
But the network they identified was fairly complicated. Was it a rare example? Or is perfect resilience impossible in many other networks as well?
Minor Problems
The 2012 paper caught the attention of Stefan Schmid, a networking researcher now at the Technical University of Berlin. He toyed with the perfect-resilience problem on and off for years, but his first real progress came in 2020, when he and his colleagues made a connection to a topic in mathematics called the theory of graph minors.
Computer scientists have long studied the mathematical properties of real-world networks by modeling them as graphs — webs of nodes connected by lines called edges. Imagine that you start with a graph, then repeatedly simplify it using three basic operations: You can delete a node, delete an edge, or merge pairs of connected nodes. The graphs that you can obtain by combining these operations are known as the minors of the larger graph.
These operations never make it more likely that packets will get routed in endless loops. If a graph is perfectly resilient, then so are all of its minors.
You can reverse this logic and understand the behavior of large, complex graphs using the properties of their simpler minors. An iconic result in graph theory, called the Robertson-Seymour theorem, tells you what you can learn from this kind of reversal. Applied to network resilience, the theorem states that there’s only a finite number of minors that are not perfectly resilient — every larger graph that lacks perfect resilience reduces to one of these so-called forbidden minors. If you can identify the full set of forbidden minors, you’ll have a complete understanding of when perfect resilience is achievable.
Unfortunately, the Robertson-Seymour theorem doesn’t tell you how many forbidden minors there are, or how to find them. “We know such a finite set exists,” said Matthias Bentert, a theoretical computer scientist at the Technical University of Berlin and Schmid’s collaborator on the new paper. “But we don’t know, does it contain one or two graphs, or does it contain 100,000 graphs?”
The researchers wanted to find the complete set of forbidden minors and prove that no others existed.
In their 2020 paper, Schmid and his colleagues identified two simple graph minors that prevent perfect resilience, but then they got stuck. Schmid suspected they’d need a collaborator with more expertise in graph theory to make further progress. Three years later, he met Bentert at a research retreat, and they worked together briefly on a different problem. In 2025, when Bentert was wrapping up a postdoctoral fellowship in Norway, Schmid invited him to join his group in Berlin.
“It was a really perfect match,” Schmid said. “Matthias made a lot of very fast contributions on a couple of our problems.” Perhaps he’d help make quick work of the perfect-resilience problem, too.
Escaping the Maze
Bentert quickly identified a third forbidden minor. He then decided to see how far he could get by attacking the problem from the other direction. Perhaps if there were no additional forbidden minors — if the three they had found were the complete set — then he could prove that all graphs that lacked these three could be made perfectly resilient.
The strategy worked, but not in the way he had hoped. “I found that, actually, I cannot show it, because it’s not true,” Bentert said. He had discovered a fourth obstruction.
So now they had four forbidden graph structures. Were there more? Bentert tried the same strategy again: Prove that all graphs that lacked these four minors could be made perfectly resilient. The strategy worked, this time because he really had found the full set.
Bentert hadn’t expected the answer to be so simple. “I would have stopped if I reached 50 or so, but that it’s really only four was a little bit of a surprise to me,” he said.
Of course, knowing that perfect resilience is theoretically achievable for any given network is only useful if you know how to choose the right routing rules. Fortunately, Schmid and Bentert’s new result also yields a fast algorithm for finding these rules, which turn out to take a similar form in any network. They’re all based on a trick for escaping mazes: Simply take a right turn at every intersection. The only networks where a maze navigation–based approach fails are those containing one of the four forbidden minors. For those networks, changing the rules won’t help.
Real-World Resilience
With their new result, Schmid and Bentert have fully resolved the perfect-resilience problem as it was originally posed in 2012. But the solution isn’t all good news. Even though there are only four graph structures that obstruct perfect resilience, the fact that they’re so simple means that many networks will have them as minors. Dense networks with many connections are especially likely to lack perfect resilience — an ironic outcome, given that adding more links to a network is the most straightforward way to make it more reliable.
“The more connectivity you have, the more possible subgraphs there are,” Godfrey said. “I wouldn’t be surprised if many real-world networks do not have a solution for perfect resilience.”
That may not be a deal-breaker: In some communication networks, resilience isn’t as critical as high speed and low congestion, two factors that Schmid and Bentert’s rules don’t take into account. And in cases where resilience is important, Schmid and Bentert’s result may not be the end of the story. They now plan to study how the situation changes if each packet can carry a record of the last few nodes it visited. Bentert is optimistic that this approach could make perfect resilience achievable for a broader range of networks, yet still remain feasible in the real world.
“Maybe some very freaky networks will not be perfectly resilient” even in a modified version of the problem, he said. “But everything that will ever be designed by a human or a machine will be.”
