OpenAI · November 23, 2026 edition
The November 24 preprints in family 379, Euclidean tensor geometry and its applications to complexity and combinatorics, subsume the results of this preprint. Paths, trees and grids separate Valiant’s hierarchy proves the separation as part of the full arithmetic hierarchy over every field. Circuit lower bounds for Hamiltonian cycle and the permanent strengthens the quantitative lower bounds for both polynomials, with the same characteristic restriction for the permanent.
Theorem 1.1 gives a border arithmetic circuit size lower bound of
$\exp(\Omega((\log n)^{5/4}))$ for an explicit VNP family over every field.
Corollary 1.2 transfers the bound to the directed Hamiltonian cycle polynomial
over every field and to the permanent outside characteristic two.

Mozilla released Firefox 161 on Tuesday with a new setting you can use to choose which pages automatically open with the browser’s VPN active. Using the “Manage VPN rules” option in Firefox’s VPN panel, you can set it to “always on” or “always off” for specific sites, so you don’t have to toggle it manually every time you visit certain pages.
Now Firefox can select which sites use its VPN, and clear your browsing history with one click
The new ‘Fire’ button can wipe history, cookies, and other data right from your toolbar.
Starting Tuesday, Mozilla is also rolling out a “Fire” button in standard Firefox windows that lets you quickly clear your browsing data directly from the toolbar. You can choose which data it deletes, including browsing history, downloads history, cookie data, site data, temporary files, saved form info, and website permissions and preferences. If you set the button to delete all of that data, clicking it will sign you out of everything and open a fresh Firefox window.
Tuesday’s Firefox update also adds an option for creating a keyboard shortcut for copying your current tab’s URL, and brings its “read aloud” option in Reader Mode to the Android version of Firefox. Alongside the update, Mozilla says Firefox is also now available directly through the Play Store on cars with Google built-in.

Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.

A Day in the Life of a Senior Leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:28:20 UTC
03:28:20 KST

One of many unexpected benefits of Ask Rands is that having a robot answer questions from the internet about all of your writing helps you discover contradictions. I’ve flip-flopped on whether a leader should code, and Grumbles knows this and explains it:
Yes, and he did it out loud. In “Technicality” (2007), Rands lays out his old new-manager rule, “Stop coding,” then says: “Too bad I’m wrong.” He adds, “Not totally,” and jokes he might need to call past co-workers to apologize. That’s not a flip-flop so much as a signed confession.
Another evolution. I stopped using the word managers and started using the word leaders. This is problematic, as the book most folks know is called “Managing Humans.” Gotta say it — love that punchy title, but how does that square with one of my favorite pithy sayings: “Managers tell you where you are. Leaders tell you where you are going”?
So, which is it, Rands? Leaders or managers?
Wait for it.
The End of the Trilogy
I’m delighted (relieved) to report that I wrote another book. I’m calling it the end of the trilogy because the first O’Reilly book, Software Developer’s Career Handbook, focuses on getting into leadership; the second one, The Art of Leadership, worked on second-level managers often known as Directors, and this one focuses on a day in the life of the senior leaders, the Executives.
There was no grand plan to do a trilogy. The writing mostly comes from this blog, and over the years that I wrote, I was a front-line manager, a Director, and an Executive. The writing reflects the experience.
A Day in the Life contains the most original writing of any of the books, including original sections for your Morning, Afternoon, Evening, and Night. I had a large amount of help from Grumbles, who wrote none of the words, but was incredibly handy with technical and organizational issues. Thanks, Grumbles!
I’d also like to thank Charity Majors, who wrote the foreword for this book; my favorite line:
Stories train the LLM between your ears.
It’s Both
If you read my pithy saying as a ding on managers, you’re right. That was the original intent. At the time, I was frustrated with the managers who just managed. Just told me where we were. Assessed the current situation. And didn’t seem to care about the future. Leadership, the act of imagining a better future and figuring out how to get there, seemed much more relevant and helpful.
It’s both. There are times when you need to manage and an equal number of times when you need to lead. A great manager is who I need to be when the sky is starting to fall. This is a human who knows how to handle the disaster. They aren’t going to prevent it, but that’s work for later when everyone has calmed down.
And then there are times we require a great leader. Close your eyes and imagine a leader you admire. Tell me a story about them. I bet you have a story about an awe-inspiring accomplishment or perhaps a product they built. Or advice they gave you at just the right time.
These impressive leaders — they are just humans… like you. What they do differently is that they’ve built a set of habits that give them time, space, and tools to lead. This book is not about grand accomplishments; it’s about how to find that time, build that space, and refine the tools.

“Pervert glasses" named word of the year by Macquarie Dictionary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:21:01 UTC
03:21:01 KST

Each year, the Macquarie Dictionary calls together a select Committee to discuss the new words and definitions that have entered the Macquarie Dictionary over the past year. The aim of this is to select one of these to be awarded the Committee’s Choice Word of the Year.
As part of this process, our editors create a longlist of words across 13 categories which, over the course of a few hours, are whittled down into a shortlist. And from this, the Word of the Year is chosen.
The Committee this year was comprised of:
- Editorial Team at Macquarie Dictionary
- David Astle – crossword maker, radio host, and writer
- Tiger Webb – language research specialist, ABC
The shortlist is then opened to the public to register what you think the Word of the Year should be. The word with the most votes is awarded the People’s Choice Word of the Year.
You can review the final shortlist here (and for those interested, the longlist here). Thank you for helping us decide on the defining new word of 2026!
Macquarie Dictionary Word of the Year 2026
2026 has undeniably been another year of rapid technological development, especially in the world of AI, as it finds its way into more and more parts of our lives. This year’s Word of the Year winner and runners up reflect this continued development, but also recognise that life does continue in and around our changing world.
Committee Winner
PERVERT GLASSES
plural noun Colloquial camera glasses; smart glasses.
[from the use by some of filming or taking photos of others without their knowledge or consent]
‘The coinage pervert glasses is a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026 in so many ways. On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname pervert glasses mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development. The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.’
–THE COMMITTEE
Committee Honourable Mentions
PMOS
noun (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome) a disorder, possibly genetic, leading to irregularities in ovulation and menstruation in women; associated with acne, excess hair growth, insulin resistance, and obesity. Formerly known as PCOS (polycystic ovarian syndrome).
‘As awareness of medical misogyny (a WOTY 2025 honourable mention) spreads, we hope to see more terms like PMOS entering the dictionary. It shows the power that language can hold, both negatively in the problems caused by the commonly misleading term PCOS, and positively in how this decade-long Australian-led campaign to rename this condition was recently adopted worldwide.’
–THE COMMITTEE
AGENTIC
adjective (especially of artificial intelligence) able to act or make decisions independently.
‘While it might not be the most flashy, funny, or socially impactful word on the surface, agentic has seen an exponential increase in usage over the last 12 months. Where 2024 and 2025 saw the development and massive spread of large language models, the release of agentic AI tools such as OpenClaw and the mischief they recently wrought has brought this otherwise very technical term firmly into the mainstream.’
–THE COMMITTEE
MARRICKVILLE PAUSE
noun Colloquial a temporary halt in conversation by people in the inner-west suburbs of Sydney, to await the passing of a loud, low-flying aircraft, after which the conversation continues.
[so called because the suburb Marrickville lies directly beneath a flight path, in very close proximity to the international airport]
‘It is undeniable that we are facing major cultural shifts in the digital world, and as a result, seeing huge language innovation at an international scale. Marrickville pause represents a departure from this trend – a highly localised term for a purely physical phenomenon, but one that is so universally experienced by people who spend time in the area.’
–THE COMMITTEE
People’s Choice Winner
And we have a threepeat! For the third year running, the public have aligned with the Committee’s choice by selecting pervert glasses to be crowned People’s Choice Word of the Year 2026!
PERVERT GLASSES
plural noun Colloquial camera glasses; smart glasses.
[from the use by some of filming or taking photos of others without their knowledge or consent]
People’s Choice Honourable Mentions
DIGITAL DEMENTIA
noun a supposed condition characterised by short-term memory loss, attention deficit, impaired decision-making, etc., thought to result from an excessive reliance on digital devices and artificial intelligence.
‘Digital dementia is, of course, not a real medical diagnosis but that hasn’t stopped the fear of an increasing reliance on digital devices from resonating deeply. People are finding that they’re struggling to navigate without Google Maps and to make and remember plans without iCal. It will be interesting to see if all of this outsourcing does in fact lead to impaired cognition in the long term.’
–THE COMMITTEE
AI;DR
interjection Colloquial a term used by a reader to indicate to others that an online item has been created by AI and is not worth reading.
[AI + d(on’t) or d(idn’t) r(ead); modelled on TL;DR]
‘A nice play on TL;DR (a code for too long; didn’t read), AI;DR gives fellow readers an instant heads-up that the text to follow is what they consider to be AI slop. As the sheer volume of AI generated text is ever-increasing, this succinct code will become a much-welcomed time saver.’
–THE COMMITTEE

“Pervert glasses" named word of the year by Macquarie Dictionary

Each year, the Macquarie Dictionary calls together a select Committee to discuss the new words and definitions that have entered the Macquarie Dictionary over the past year. The aim of this is to select one of these to be awarded the Committee’s Choice Word of the Year.
As part of this process, our editors create a longlist of words across 13 categories which, over the course of a few hours, are whittled down into a shortlist. And from this, the Word of the Year is chosen.
The Committee this year was comprised of:
- Editorial Team at Macquarie Dictionary
- David Astle – crossword maker, radio host, and writer
- Tiger Webb – language research specialist, ABC
The shortlist is then opened to the public to register what you think the Word of the Year should be. The word with the most votes is awarded the People’s Choice Word of the Year.
You can review the final shortlist here (and for those interested, the longlist here). Thank you for helping us decide on the defining new word of 2026!
Macquarie Dictionary Word of the Year 2026
2026 has undeniably been another year of rapid technological development, especially in the world of AI, as it finds its way into more and more parts of our lives. This year’s Word of the Year winner and runners up reflect this continued development, but also recognise that life does continue in and around our changing world.
Committee Winner
PERVERT GLASSES
plural noun Colloquial camera glasses; smart glasses.
[from the use by some of filming or taking photos of others without their knowledge or consent]
‘The coinage pervert glasses is a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026 in so many ways. On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname pervert glasses mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development. The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.’
–THE COMMITTEE

noun (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome) a disorder, possibly genetic, leading to irregularities in ovulation and menstruation in women; associated with acne, excess hair growth, insulin resistance, and obesity. Formerly known as PCOS (polycystic ovarian syndrome).
‘As awareness of medical misogyny (a WOTY 2025 honourable mention) spreads, we hope to see more terms like PMOS entering the dictionary. It shows the power that language can hold, both negatively in the problems caused by the commonly misleading term PCOS, and positively in how this decade-long Australian-led campaign to rename this condition was recently adopted worldwide.’
–THE COMMITTEE
AGENTIC
adjective (especially of artificial intelligence) able to act or make decisions independently.
‘While it might not be the most flashy, funny, or socially impactful word on the surface, agentic has seen an exponential increase in usage over the last 12 months. Where 2024 and 2025 saw the development and massive spread of large language models, the release of agentic AI tools such as OpenClaw and the mischief they recently wrought has brought this otherwise very technical term firmly into the mainstream.’
–THE COMMITTEE
MARRICKVILLE PAUSE
noun Colloquial a temporary halt in conversation by people in the inner-west suburbs of Sydney, to await the passing of a loud, low-flying aircraft, after which the conversation continues.
[so called because the suburb Marrickville lies directly beneath a flight path, in very close proximity to the international airport]
‘It is undeniable that we are facing major cultural shifts in the digital world, and as a result, seeing huge language innovation at an international scale. Marrickville pause represents a departure from this trend – a highly localised term for a purely physical phenomenon, but one that is so universally experienced by people who spend time in the area.’
–THE COMMITTEE

David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:12:33 UTC
03:12:33 KST

Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.
David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.
Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”
Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.
It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.
Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.
At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.
Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.
Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:02:59 UTC
03:02:59 KST

The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.
The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post.
The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.
The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.
While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.
“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.
The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.
The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”
The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

Mayo Clinic To Give Appointment Workers 5 Paid Minutes a Day To Boot Up Computers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Mayo Clinic To Give Appointment Workers 5 Paid Minutes a Day To Boot Up Computers (cbsnews.com) 53
			
		 	
				Mayo Clinic has agreed to pay more than $906,000 in back wages to employees who schedule patient appointments. An investigation by Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison found that employees were performing unpaid work before and after their shifts, including time spent booting up computers and finishing patient calls. Under the settlement (PDF), Mayo will stop rounding employees' work hours and give them five paid minutes at the start of each shift to boot up their computers. CBS News reports:  In a statement, Mayo Clinic said it reached the agreement to resolve concerns about "certain timekeeping practices" involving a group of the specialists. The clinic said it doesn't agree with the attorney general's position but decided that a resolution in which money went to its staff, rather than to defense fees, was preferable. Mayo said it is committed to paying employees accurately and appropriately and reviews its compensation policies regularly. Neither the announcement nor the statement says how many workers are covered or how far back the unpaid time goes.
"Under Minnesota law, workers need to be compensated for all the time they work," Ellison said. State law requires employers to pay employees for all time spent on duties connected to their jobs, including time on the employer's premises. Ellison said Mayo cooperated with the investigation and changed its policies on its own to pay workers for the time. He said other employers should take note: "they're on the clock and need to be paid" if they are on site or doing work duties. Ellison encouraged any worker who believes they're being underpaid to contact his office, saying it may be able to help co-workers as well.

Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:44:34 UTC
02:44:34 KST

It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.
While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.
The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.
In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.
The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.
Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

Electric truck startup Harbinger gets financing boost from Palmer Luckey’s bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:29:09 UTC
02:29:09 KST

Harbinger has tapped Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank as a new source of capital as the electric truck startup looks to diversify how it funds its growth and an expanding portfolio of products spanning autonomous vehicles, energy storage, and defense.
Los Angeles-based Harbinger said Tuesday it secured more than $100 million in financing, including a convertible note from Pinegrove Venture Partners and senior debt from Erebor Bank, which launched in February 2026 and recently surpassed $1 billion in loans, according to the Financial Times.
The new financing comes less than three weeks after Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D funding round co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline. FedEx, which ordered 2,000 trucks from Harbinger, also participated.
Harbinger co-founder and chief executive John Harris explained in a statement that building an industrial technology company at scale requires a “different financing approach,” adding that the capital needed to ramp up production and deliver vehicles to customers shouldn’t have to come entirely from equity. Harris noted that major vehicle and aerospace manufacturers have long relied on debt financing to support their production operations.
Erebor is now Harbinger’s primary banking partner. In a statement, Luckey said traditional lenders have struggled to support the unique capital needs of businesses developing real technology and creating U.S. jobs.
“Harbinger is exactly the kind of business we built Erebor to back: an American manufacturer building world-class technology,” he said.

Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:17:09 UTC
02:17:09 KST

Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen.
Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
The music streaming platform estimates that it will delete 29 million songs as a result of the AI ban.
The move comes just months after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing tracks identified as 100 percent AI-generated. In a post on X, Andersen says Tidal needed to take a more “drastic” measure, as AI music made up 43 percent of the tracks distributed to the platform in the last 90 days. “We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all,” Andersen adds.
Bandcamp similarly banned AI music earlier this year, while other music streaming platforms attempt to address a flood of AI songs by applying new labels or removing them from user algorithms. Spotify recently announced that it removed 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from recommendations over the past year, and also launched new “AI persona” badges for artists that use an AI identity. YouTube has rolled out AI music labels as well, while Apple Music is planning to launch AI labels this year. Meanwhile, Deezer is giving users the option to filter out AI music.
“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal says in a separate post on X.
The platform is also going to ban music distributors from submitting AI songs, using the AI detection tool Ircam Amplify and metadata checks to reject submissions generated solely with AI. Tidal notes that it won’t ban songs made with the assistance of AI tools, as long as AI doesn’t make up the “sole output.”

Top MIT Physicist: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About 'Taking over the World'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:10:45 UTC
02:10:45 KST

Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist
Apparently they discuss overthrowing the US government after a few drinks.
by Clare Hymer
24 November 2026
Employees at US artificial intelligence company Anthropic openly talk about “overthrowing the US government” and “taking over the world”, a world-renowned physicist has claimed.
In an interview with Novara Media, Max Tegmark, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said: “When I talk to people who work for Anthropic, after they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world.”
“They tend to not use words like ‘coup’ and ‘overthrow the US government’. They instead use the code phrase ‘alignment without control’,” he said.
‘Alignment without control’ is the idea that AI should be kept in check by being instilled with certain values – likely those shared by Anthropic, Tegmark said – rather than being directly controlled by humans.
“We get the sort of future that Alan Turing predicted, where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine-god running Earth, and then the rest of us just have to hope that somehow it’s gonna be nice.”
Turing, widely regarded as the founder of computer science, famously warned in 1951 that once machines started thinking, we should expect them to take control.
Tegmark said the comments from Anthropic staff should alarm anyone who cares about democracy. “These companies really don’t seem to like it [democracy]. They have lobbied really hard to even prevent any meaningful government oversight of them,” he said.

Meta brings its Muse AI assistant directly into Instagram DMs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday. The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.
The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.
Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.
Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.
Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.
Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.
Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.
Meta says that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram. Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

GTA 6 Hacker Released On License With Warning 'Don't Let This Happen Again' (bbc.com) 36
			
		 	
				Arion Kurtaj, the 21-year-old Lapsus$ hacker responsible for the 2022 leak of Grand Theft Auto VI, was released on license the same day he was sentenced to seven years in prison. He is subject to a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting his online activities, including banning him from Telegram and Discord. "You are a very talented young man," the judge told Kurtaj, warning him: "Don't let this happen again." The BBC reports:  [...] With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse. He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week. He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker. Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5 million to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time. The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman -- a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:46:00 UTC
01:46:00 KST

Music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision.
Tidal said it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the new rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day.
Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.
The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.
The move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, said that it will introduce a toggle to let users filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this issue, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures.
Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, said on X.
The company said that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams.
“It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases. But this situation is different – at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried,” the company said in a post.
Meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%.

Uber and Nuro have started testing driverless Lucid Gravity SUVs on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area more than six months after receiving the permit that allowed the companies to pull the human safety driver from behind the wheel.
The companies will soon begin offering driverless rides to employees in the final lead-up to launching a commercial robotaxi service in the first quarter of 2027.
The milestone comes just 16 months after Uber announced an ambitious plan to launch a premium robotaxi service using Lucid electric vehicles outfitted with autonomous vehicle technology developed by startup Nuro.
That plan came with hefty investments in both companies and much-needed endorsements of their respective products. Uber initially agreed to invest $300 million in Lucid — a figure that has since ballooned to $500 million. Uber also agreed to invest nearly $500 million in Nuro, TechCrunch previously reported, citing sources familiar with the deal.
The agreement provided both Lucid and Nuro with boosts beyond the obvious capital injection. Uber agreed to buy at least 20,000 of Lucid Gravity SUVs over the next six years (a figure that later popped to at least 35,000 vehicles), giving the struggling EV maker a more predictable source of revenue. Nuro, meanwhile, was less than a year removed from announcing a risky, but necessary pivot away from developing driverless delivery vehicles and toward licensing its autonomous vehicle technology to automakers and mobility companies.
Nuro has spent nearly a year testing the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with a human safety operator behind the wheel. The California Department of Motor Vehicles, the agency that regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, granted Nuro a driverless AV permit in May 2026.
Uber and Nuro are also testing autonomous vehicles on public roads in Houston with human safety operators behind the wheel. Nuro is supplementing that on-road testing with closed-course testing and simulation to validate the self-driving system before opening the robotaxis to the public. The companies’ combined engineering fleet of autonomous vehicles, which stood at 100 AVs earlier this year, is expanding as Lucid begins manufacturing the first production versions of the robotaxis at its Arizona factory.
The Lucid Gravity robotaxi, unveiled in January 2026, is outfitted with high-resolution cameras, solid-state lidar sensors, and radars that help the self-driving system perceive the real-world environment and operate in it. Uber, which will own and operate the fleet, has focused its efforts on the in-cabin experience, including how riders will interact with the vehicle.

US Commerce Department adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist as Huang retakes control of Nvidia

Cyberattack campaign compromising Check Point servers across 22 organizations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:32:17 UTC
01:32:17 KST

GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.
Campaign Summary
- GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.
- We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims.
- The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.
- We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin.
- The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers.
- The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.
- The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).
- Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets.
- Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing.
- We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims.
Observed Attacker Activities
We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
HFS Scanning and Exploitation
The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.
Example POST to loginSrp1 and response
Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested
2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.
Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie
Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.
2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.
On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.
Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop
2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.
Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.
Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.
The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.
Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant
They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.
2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.
The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.
Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration
Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.
Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.
The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.
2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.
Excerpt from exploit.py - This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.
2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.
Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.
2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.
Excerpt from pull_<redacted_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.
2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.
2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.
- CVE-2020-1472 (Microsoft Netlogon),
- CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Netscaler),
- CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure),
- CVE-2021-26855/34473 (Microsoft Exchange) and
- CVE-2021-21972 / CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter)
2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.
Excerpt from comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_spray.py
2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.
Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.
All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.
Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt
One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.
After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.
Protecting Their Access
2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.
Excerpt from cve_2026_98432.py
Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.
Notes on Attack Timeframe and Timeline
- The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets.
- We observed GT13 attack activity between 2026-10-02 13:17:45 and 2026-11-02 03:19:46 UTC. During our observation of the actor, we did not observe any adversary hands-on-keyboard activity between ~17:00 UTC and ~00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 UTC hour. We know the risks of time zone analysis and do not put much weight into the actor’s tendency to operate in what would be a convenient UTC+7- or UTC+8 workday.
- The attack infrastructure was long established before we first saw it, as we note the attempted malware domain newpayapp[.]com was first registered on 2026-03-13 12:46:28 UTC. It may be a UTC+7-friendly coincidence that the domain was originally created with the registrant state as “Hai Phong” with country code “VN” (see Cloudflare’s RDAP service).
- We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.

====================================================================================================

Cyberattack campaign compromising Check Point servers across 22 organizations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:32:17 UTC
01:32:17 KST

GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.
Campaign Summary
- GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.
- We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims.
- The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.
- We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin.
- The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers.
- The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.
- The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).
- Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets.
- Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing.
- We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims.
Observed Attacker Activities
We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
HFS Scanning and Exploitation
The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.
Example POST to loginSrp1 and response
Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested
2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.
Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie
Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.
2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.
On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.
Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop
2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.
Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.
Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.
The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.
Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant
They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.
2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.
The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.
Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration
Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.
Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.
The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.
2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.
Excerpt from exploit.py - This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.
2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.
Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.
2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.
Excerpt from pull_<redacted_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.
2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.
2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.
- CVE-2020-1472 (Microsoft Netlogon),
- CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Netscaler),
- CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure),
- CVE-2021-26855/34473 (Microsoft Exchange) and
- CVE-2021-21972 / CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter)
2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.
Excerpt from comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_comb.py
Excerpt from ssh_spray.py
2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.
Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.
All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.
Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt
One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.
After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.
Protecting Their Access
2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.
Excerpt from cve_2026_98432.py
Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.
Notes on Attack Timeframe and Timeline
- The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets.
- We observed GT13 attack activity between 2026-10-02 13:17:45 and 2026-11-02 03:19:46 UTC. During our observation of the actor, we did not observe any adversary hands-on-keyboard activity between ~17:00 UTC and ~00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 UTC hour. We know the risks of time zone analysis and do not put much weight into the actor’s tendency to operate in what would be a convenient UTC+7- or UTC+8 workday.
- The attack infrastructure was long established before we first saw it, as we note the attempted malware domain newpayapp[.]com was first registered on 2026-03-13 12:46:28 UTC. It may be a UTC+7-friendly coincidence that the domain was originally created with the registrant state as “Hai Phong” with country code “VN” (see Cloudflare’s RDAP service).
- We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.
