Jetty Pro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:23:02 UTC
01:23:02 KST

Hypercritical
Jetty Pro
My first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing, the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing (and classic Mac OS).
After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales).
Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace, which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files. Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse!
Alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner.
This is not a hard problem to solve. Plenty of Mac apps can provide something close to what I want…but not exactly what I want, in the specific way that I want it. For many years, I got by with some folders in the corner of my desktop. But the problem nagged at me.
A few years ago, I went so far as to implement my desired feature in SwitchGlass, adding the ability to create a small, extra palette full of folders in addition to the app switcher. But it felt incongruous with the rest of the app, so I never shipped it. And I didn’t want to maintain my own private fork of SwitchGlass, so I abandoned that branch of the code.
How It Started
Today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of new, niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. Even for experienced software developers, vibe coding has made it possible to create apps that were previously “not worth building” due to an unfavorable ratio of effort to payoff.
It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right?
That was three and a half months ago.
How It’s Going
So what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed.
I began the project by feeding a coding agent the source code to my app, SwitchGlass, as a starting point. I wrote SwitchGlass six years ago using a substantially more primitive version of SwiftUI. (For the developers out there, it predates @Observable and @State, and it supports Macs all the way back to macOS 12 Monterey from 2021.) I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display.
It worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess…
Now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock.
Only Apple…
If you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews, you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.)
To pick just one example, I’ve always wanted clicking on a folder in the Dock to open that folder in the Finder. The Dock did work this way for several years, but in 2009’s Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard (…I think?), Apple switched to requiring a Command-Option-click to open a folder in the Finder. Since then, I’ve been Command-Option-clicking folders in the Dock many, many times per day. It’s a small thing, but it adds up: seventeen years of Command-Option clicking!
But what could I do? I was forced to continue to use the Dock because there are so many things that “only the Dock can do” in macOS. I was reminded of this harsh reality when I created SwitchGlass. Why doesn’t SwitchGlass show notification badges? Why does the Calendar icon show today’s date in the Dock but not in SwitchGlass? Why don’t app icons in SwitchGlass bounce when the app needs attention? Why can’t I quit an app from SwitchGlass?
Though I did find a workaround for that last one, the answer to most of these questions is that third-party apps simply can’t do all the things the Dock can do. The Dock is part of the operating system, and it enjoys special privileges and deep integration that no third-party app can match.
This remains true today, especially for sandboxed apps sold through the Mac App Store like SwitchGlass (and all my other Mac apps). But what about apps that aren’t in the Mac App Store? What about unsandboxed apps? How close can they come to doing all the things the Dock does, especially if they use private APIs that are forbidden in the Mac App Store?
I aimed to find out. I hatched a plan, which I announced on episode 706 of Accidental Tech Podcast on August 26, 2026. I would create two apps: one called Jetty that would be sold through the Mac App Store, and a more powerful, unsandboxed app called Jetty Pro that would be distributed directly to customers, outside the Mac App Store.
But as I worked on the two apps, it became clear that “plain Jetty” was not that great. It had all the same limitations as SwitchGlass when it came to duplicating the features of the Dock. After less than two weeks of work, I abandoned plain Jetty and concentrated entirely on Jetty Pro.
After three and a half months of work, there are still things that only the Dock can do, but the list is not very long. I don’t expect most users to fully replace the Dock with Jetty Pro, but I’m happily doing so. If only my 2001 self could see me now!
Jetty Pro
Now, finally, I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. Here are some of the highlights:
- Jetty Pro palettes are extensively customizable. Nearly every palette layout metric can be adjusted. Jetty Pro can simulate the Dock backgrounds from macOS 15, 26, and 27, and it provides several of its own background appearances as well. The image at the top of this post shows just some of the possibilities.
- Jetty Pro lets you customize the icon of any item in a palette—even the Finder. And if you’ve ever wanted to break an app out of Squircle Jail, now you can do it.
- Unlike the macOS Dock, Jetty Pro will show folder label colors (without also setting a folder symbol). You can even apply color labels to folders independent of their labels in the Finder.
- Don’t want to see “Running in Background” apps in macOS 27? Jetty Pro can hide them.
- Want to hide notification badges for specific apps, but only in specific palettes? Jetty Pro can do that. And unlike the Dock, Jetty Pro can even hide notification badges on the System Settings app.
- Jetty Pro can exclude or include running apps of your choice on a per-palette basis.
- Jetty Pro lets you choose what happens when you click (or modifier-click) an app or folder in a palette.
- A Jetty Pro palette can be configured to appear on a single display, selected displays, or on every display, while also choosing which attributes, like size and position, are allowed to vary per display.
- Use Jetty Pro to augment the macOS Dock with additional palettes, or use it to replace the Dock entirely. It’s up to you.
Jetty Pro is available for a special introductory price of $9.99 per year (plus applicable taxes) until the end of 2026, with a 14-day free trial.
To learn more, including why a subscription is the only way to pay for Jetty Pro, please read the extensive documentation.
As you might have already guessed, Jetty Pro uses every private API it can get its hands on, and it requires a ton of special permissions, all of which are explained in the documentation. For sensible security reasons, macOS makes it (increasingly) cumbersome for users to grant these permissions. But Jetty Pro needs them to do what it does. Check Settings > General in Jetty Pro and make sure it says “All permissions have been granted” at the bottom. If not, click the “Details…” button for further instructions.
After a brief dalliance with more “mainstream” apps like Hyperspace, I’m back to making niche apps for Mac weirdos like me. To thine own self be true, I guess. I hope there are others out there who have longed to make the Dock work just slightly differently and are now able to do so thanks to Jetty Pro.
I’m sure many people reading this will think it’s ridiculous that I spent months battling the limitations of macOS to create what appears (to the undiscerning eye) to be a nearly identical clone of the Dock. What a waste of time! And what took so long anyway? This is a weekend project, at most!
First, I can assure you that the “simple” appearance of Jetty Pro belies the huge level of complexity and trickery required to do so many different things that macOS does not support and actively works against. If Jetty Pro really does seem simple in use, then I have done my job well. (And if you can see the seams, then that’s where I’ve failed to completely overcome a hostile system that doesn’t want to allow Jetty Pro to do what it needs to do.)
Second, I put a tremendous amount of time and effort into Jetty Pro. The documentation alone (which, like every word in every post on this website, was written by me and me alone) took weeks to create. During the lead up to Jetty Pro 1.0, I’ve released over 160 builds to my 250 beta testers—more than one build per day. The Jetty Pro app icon was created by the fine humans at The Iconfactory. From the start, I’ve treated Jetty Pro like a “real” app, not a throwaway vibe-coded project.
Having spent so many years with the Dock as a tiny pebble in my shoe, the difference between it and Jetty Pro means everything to me. Like Front and Center and SwitchGlass before it, I’m now running Jetty Pro all day, every day on my Mac. Replacing the Dock with Jetty Pro has made me happier than any other app I’ve created. I hope it will make some other Mac weirdos happy too.

====================================================================================================

After three and a half months of work, there are still things that only the Dock can do, but the list is not very long. I don’t expect most users to fully replace the Dock with Jetty Pro, but I’m happily doing so. If only my 2001 self could see me now!
Jetty Pro
Now, finally, I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. Here are some of the highlights:
- Jetty Pro palettes are extensively customizable. Nearly every palette layout metric can be adjusted. Jetty Pro can simulate the Dock backgrounds from macOS 15, 26, and 27, and it provides several of its own background appearances as well. The image at the top of this post shows just some of the possibilities.
- Jetty Pro lets you customize the icon of any item in a palette—even the Finder. And if you’ve ever wanted to break an app out of Squircle Jail, now you can do it.
- Unlike the macOS Dock, Jetty Pro will show folder label colors (without also setting a folder symbol). You can even apply color labels to folders independent of their labels in the Finder.
- Don’t want to see “Running in Background” apps in macOS 27? Jetty Pro can hide them.
- Want to hide notification badges for specific apps, but only in specific palettes? Jetty Pro can do that. And unlike the Dock, Jetty Pro can even hide notification badges on the System Settings app.
- Jetty Pro can exclude or include running apps of your choice on a per-palette basis.
- Jetty Pro lets you choose what happens when you click (or modifier-click) an app or folder in a palette.
- A Jetty Pro palette can be configured to appear on a single display, selected displays, or on every display, while also choosing which attributes, like size and position, are allowed to vary per display.
- Use Jetty Pro to augment the macOS Dock with additional palettes, or use it to replace the Dock entirely. It’s up to you.
Jetty Pro is available for a special introductory price of $9.99 per year (plus applicable taxes) until the end of 2026, with a 14-day free trial.
To learn more, including why a subscription is the only way to pay for Jetty Pro, please read the extensive documentation.
As you might have already guessed, Jetty Pro uses every private API it can get its hands on, and it requires a ton of special permissions, all of which are explained in the documentation. For sensible security reasons, macOS makes it (increasingly) cumbersome for users to grant these permissions. But Jetty Pro needs them to do what it does. Check Settings > General in Jetty Pro and make sure it says “All permissions have been granted” at the bottom. If not, click the “Details…” button for further instructions.
After a brief dalliance with more “mainstream” apps like Hyperspace, I’m back to making niche apps for Mac weirdos like me. To thine own self be true, I guess. I hope there are others out there who have longed to make the Dock work just slightly differently and are now able to do so thanks to Jetty Pro.
I’m sure many people reading this will think it’s ridiculous that I spent months battling the limitations of macOS to create what appears (to the undiscerning eye) to be a nearly identical clone of the Dock. What a waste of time! And what took so long anyway? This is a weekend project, at most!
First, I can assure you that the “simple” appearance of Jetty Pro belies the huge level of complexity and trickery required to do so many different things that macOS does not support and actively works against. If Jetty Pro really does seem simple in use, then I have done my job well. (And if you can see the seams, then that’s where I’ve failed to completely overcome a hostile system that doesn’t want to allow Jetty Pro to do what it needs to do.)
Second, I put a tremendous amount of time and effort into Jetty Pro. The documentation alone (which, like every word in every post on this website, was written by me and me alone) took weeks to create. During the lead up to Jetty Pro 1.0, I’ve released over 160 builds to my 250 beta testers—more than one build per day. The Jetty Pro app icon was created by the fine humans at The Iconfactory. From the start, I’ve treated Jetty Pro like a “real” app, not a throwaway vibe-coded project.
Having spent so many years with the Dock as a tiny pebble in my shoe, the difference between it and Jetty Pro means everything to me. Like Front and Center and SwitchGlass before it, I’m now running Jetty Pro all day, every day on my Mac. Replacing the Dock with Jetty Pro has made me happier than any other app I’ve created. I hope it will make some other Mac weirdos happy too.

How to Make a Lovable City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:19:55 UTC
01:19:55 KST

Everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.
The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.
Sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.
Sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.
Anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte showed, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.
Create enclosed spaces
The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.
While the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.
The picture above shows the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.
Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.
London’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.
An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.
Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above shows Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.
Squares should not be too large
If a square is too large, it loses its sense of enclosure, and its buildings look strangely diminished by their surroundings. Sitte provided a rule of thumb in sizing squares: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it. The pictures above show two examples of over-large squares: the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest. Both feel demoralizingly vast, with the monumental buildings they are meant to showcase (Madrid Cathedral, and Budapest’s Hall of Art) dwindling to visual insignificance on the horizon, so that they resemble doll’s houses. In both squares, the buildings are so miniaturized that they no longer seem like enclosing walls, leaving the visitor exposed in a huge open space. This problem could be solved by making the buildings much taller, but although the square would then feel enclosed, the buildings would have become terrifyingly huge, as if meant for giants rather than human beings (the courtyard of Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris is an example of this pitfall in the wild).
Some of the world’s most famous squares are, in fact, far too large. St Peter’s Square in the Vatican, seen above, was designed by the famous artist Bernini, and it does indeed look impressive in drone footage. For human visitors, however, it is an exhausting place, overwhelming without being impressive. The Basilica looks small and stubby, exactly the opposite of the desired effect. On a summer’s day, the vast, unshaded space becomes relentlessly inhospitable, and visitors huddle under the colonnades for shelter.
By contrast, the small square in front of the Pantheon in Rome exemplifies the features Sitte prized. It is impossible to fully capture its feeling of enclosure in a two-dimensional photograph, but some sense of the intimacy of the space is apparent in the pictures above, which show how this magnifies the Pantheon. The Pantheon is a smaller building than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, but it is much bigger relative to the square. This allows it to retain its dignity, despite the fact that the level of the street has risen by 1.3 meters since Antiquity, swallowing the steps that originally led up to the entrance.
Symmetry is overrated
At the time Sitte was writing, many planners believed that harmonious spaces should have regular, symmetrical plans, an idea which remains influential today. In English we even use the confusing word ‘square’ for any enclosed public spaces, whatever their shape.
Sitte rejected this, believing that symmetrical spaces do not necessarily feel harmonious at ground level, and that asymmetry is not generally disharmonious at all. The pictures above show the perfectly symmetrical Place Vendôme in Paris. Seen from a satellite, it is visually striking and certainly neater than an irregular space. Its chamfered plan supposedly inspired the design of Chanel’s No 5 perfume bottle. Pedestrians, however, generally do not stand at the exact point at which the objective balance of the buildings is reflected in their field of vision: the various points and angles from which they do experience it may even make it feel quite awkward.
Above is the Piazza delle Erbe, a market square in Verona. This ‘square’ has an odd shape, an elongated and slightly wonky pentagon. Nobody is likely to model perfume bottles on it. But at human level, this does not matter as pedestrians can never take in all five sides at once, and so its irregular form is barely even visible. For the most part, the irregularities are ‘seen only on paper’, and to the extent they are visible, they are not experienced as imperfections. Sitte argued that they in fact serve to subtly arouse visual interest, and also create happy recesses that can host resting places, statues, or other public art.
Move monuments to the edges
If you were putting an ornament in your living room, you would be very unlikely to stand it in the middle of the carpet. It would get in the way, break up the space, and might well look lost and isolated. Nor would you place it in front of one of the room’s main features, like the fireplace. It would block the view of the fireplace, and the fireplace would be a disagreeably busy backdrop. Almost certainly, you would put it against the wall, preferably a relatively neutral wall to create a calm background.
Sitte thought the same considerations applied to the placing of sculptures, fountains, and other monuments in outdoor spaces. Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares, where they would block natural routes, break up the space, and look isolated and diminished. Nor should they be placed on axes with key buildings, where they block the view of the architecture. Instead they should line the sides, where they can stand out against relatively neutral backgrounds.
This was implicitly understood in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance, and Sitte illustrates his book with examples from all three periods. Above, for example, is the Piazza della Signoria in Florence. The numerous statues line the sides of the square, leaving the center free for people to pass through or mill about. This is advantageous for the statues too: Michelangelo’s David (today a replica, since the original was moved indoors) stands out splendidly against the plain masonry walls of the Palazzo Vecchio.
Later planners became fascinated by the apparent neatness of centering statues. Above is the Victoria Memorial in London. The Memorial stands on the main axis of the Mall, blocking the view of Buckingham Palace behind it. This is not advantageous for the Memorial either, whose outline clashes confusedly with the complex detailing of the building. If you search through pictures of the Memorial, you will notice that most photographers picture it from an awkward oblique angle, the least bad way to capture both the monument and the central pavilion of the palace.
Isolating statues against the sky is not much better. A bronze cast of David was later placed on the Piazzale Michelangelo, at the center of a wide square with stunning views over Florence. The statue is enormous, over five meters tall, but it looks strangely miniaturized in its location. Sitte remarked that contemporary tourists often came away with the drastically false impression that it was life-sized. We judge size partly by comparison, and when an object is isolated from comparators, its size becomes harder to assess. This is why the backdrop of a wall can make sculpture look bigger and grander by providing a constant visual key.
In Sitte’s view, the plain edge of a small square was not only an acceptable site for a statue, but the best one. Sitte disliked museums, which he called ‘art prisons’, and thought that only people with a ‘special mental preparation’ could enjoy art under their ‘morbid influences’. The Sittesque city would be one that teemed with art, but woven into the urban fabric as an adornment of ordinary civic life.
Buildings need context
Sitte’s view on buildings was similar. Nineteenth-century architects tended to place major public buildings in the middle of squares, judging that this gave them greater dignity. Sitte thought this ‘pedantic, futile modern practice’ destroyed the square and squandered the opportunity to frame the public building with vernacular architecture. He pointed out that many historic cities were in fact designed along the lines he proposed. Of the 255 churches of Rome, 41 adjoined other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three, and two on all four. Only six were freestanding, two of them modern churches of expatriate Protestant communities.
The most striking examples of this arose when nineteenth-century governments actually demolished the vernacular buildings that surrounded historic monuments. This practice, often known by its French name dégagement, was surprisingly common: nineteenth-century planners thought that it displayed the monuments better. It provides a useful experiment on the effect of freestanding versus adjoined monumental architecture.
For example, Notre Dame Cathedral was formerly approached through a narrow street called the Rue Neuve Notre Dame. The street was demolished by the government planner Haussmann in the nineteenth century to create the Parvis Notre-Dame, a large square that the cathedral still faces today. Haussmann intended to improve the view of the cathedral, but the effect is the opposite. The vernacular fabric formed a visual frame, defining and concentrating views onto the facade. It provided scale, making the cathedral look larger by contrast to the ordinary buildings around it. It also prevented visitors from seeing the whole facade until they were very close, close enough that it towered up terrifically before them. Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.
Sitte thought that cities should move in the opposite direction. The Votive Church in Vienna was built in the 1870s on what Sitte described as a ‘desolate monster plaza’ that was ‘intolerably exposed to high wind, inclement weather, heat and dust, as well as to the din of the streets, and the incessant clanging of trams.’ The church does indeed have an awkward and lonely feeling. Sitte thought that the architecture of the building was actually very good, and that the defects in its effect were entirely the fault of its location. He proposed building up regular urban fabric on most of the ‘monster plaza’, defining three small squares with well-framed views onto the church. Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.
Another way to understand this contrast is to look at whole cities planned on Sittesque and anti-Sittesque principles. The pictures below show Padua and Washington DC. It is as though a figure-ground switch has taken place: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings. Monumental buildings in Washington sit alone on their city blocks, untouched by vernacular fabric. Monumental buildings in Padua constantly link up with vernacular fabric to shape small, sheltered spaces from which they can be properly enjoyed.
The rise, fall, and rise of Camillo Sitte
The Art of Building Cities was an immediate success, landing, in the words of Sitte’s English translator Charles T Stewart, ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’. Within a year of publication it had prompted the redrawing of urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and Sitte was being approached by town officials seeking his advice on their own plans. By Sitte’s death in 1903, advocates of his ideas were to be found in prestigious positions in cities including Munich, Berlin, and Vienna, either teaching or as official city architects.
Two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate the effect of Sittesque ideas on urban planning. In the nineteenth century, Helsinki followed a neoclassical grid plan, with straight streets meeting at right angles. In the early twentieth century, it switched dramatically to a Sittesque approach, introducing curving streets, turbine squares, T-junctions, and asymmetrical spaces. The resulting neighborhood is full of pleasing, characterful spaces and unexpected ‘old town’ effects, even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor.
But Sitte’s influence was curiously short-lived. In the decades following Sitte’s death in 1903, European urban design came to be dominated by the modernist movement. Everything that Sitte hated about nineteenth-century planning was vastly amplified in modernism. With honorable exception, the modernists treated public space as merely whatever was left over after the buildings had been placed, and had no sympathy with Sitte’s approach of treating spaces as primary and shaping the buildings around them. Instead of lining the edge of a city block with buildings (a ‘perimeter block’) they preferred to orient all blocks in the same direction (‘parallel blocks’), often with a seemingly arbitrary angle to the street. Sitte had decried the gridiron blocks of the nineteenth century for the weakly defined spaces they created. But by twentieth-century standards, the straight ‘corridor streets’ of the nineteenth century look comparatively Sittesque.
Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.
Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘New Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. But the Sittesque revival goes far beyond this. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.
Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.
Phoebe Arslanagic-Little is a writer and policy researcher.
Samuel Hughes is an editor at Works in Progress.

Almost certainly, you would put it against the wall, preferably a relatively neutral wall to create a calm background.
Sitte thought the same considerations applied to the placing of sculptures, fountains, and other monuments in outdoor spaces. Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares, where they would block natural routes, break up the space, and look isolated and diminished. Nor should they be placed on axes with key buildings, where they block the view of the architecture. Instead they should line the sides, where they can stand out against relatively neutral backgrounds.
This was implicitly understood in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance, and Sitte illustrates his book with examples from all three periods. Above, for example, is the Piazza della Signoria in Florence. The numerous statues line the sides of the square, leaving the center free for people to pass through or mill about. This is advantageous for the statues too: Michelangelo’s David (today a replica, since the original was moved indoors) stands out splendidly against the plain masonry walls of the Palazzo Vecchio.
Later planners became fascinated by the apparent neatness of centering statues. Above is the Victoria Memorial in London. The Memorial stands on the main axis of the Mall, blocking the view of Buckingham Palace behind it. This is not advantageous for the Memorial either, whose outline clashes confusedly with the complex detailing of the building. If you search through pictures of the Memorial, you will notice that most photographers picture it from an awkward oblique angle, the least bad way to capture both the monument and the central pavilion of the palace.
Isolating statues against the sky is not much better. A bronze cast of David was later placed on the Piazzale Michelangelo, at the center of a wide square with stunning views over Florence. The statue is enormous, over five meters tall, but it looks strangely miniaturized in its location. Sitte remarked that contemporary tourists often came away with the drastically false impression that it was life-sized. We judge size partly by comparison, and when an object is isolated from comparators, its size becomes harder to assess. This is why the backdrop of a wall can make sculpture look bigger and grander by providing a constant visual key.
In Sitte’s view, the plain edge of a small square was not only an acceptable site for a statue, but the best one. Sitte disliked museums, which he called ‘art prisons’, and thought that only people with a ‘special mental preparation’ could enjoy art under their ‘morbid influences’. The Sittesque city would be one that teemed with art, but woven into the urban fabric as an adornment of ordinary civic life.
Buildings need context
Sitte’s view on buildings was similar. Nineteenth-century architects tended to place major public buildings in the middle of squares, judging that this gave them greater dignity. Sitte thought this ‘pedantic, futile modern practice’ destroyed the square and squandered the opportunity to frame the public building with vernacular architecture. He pointed out that many historic cities were in fact designed along the lines he proposed. Of the 255 churches of Rome, 41 adjoined other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three, and two on all four. Only six were freestanding, two of them modern churches of expatriate Protestant communities.
The most striking examples of this arose when nineteenth-century governments actually demolished the vernacular buildings that surrounded historic monuments. This practice, often known by its French name dégagement, was surprisingly common: nineteenth-century planners thought that it displayed the monuments better. It provides a useful experiment on the effect of freestanding versus adjoined monumental architecture.
For example, Notre Dame Cathedral was formerly approached through a narrow street called the Rue Neuve Notre Dame. The street was demolished by the government planner Haussmann in the nineteenth century to create the Parvis Notre-Dame, a large square that the cathedral still faces today. Haussmann intended to improve the view of the cathedral, but the effect is the opposite. The vernacular fabric formed a visual frame, defining and concentrating views onto the facade. It provided scale, making the cathedral look larger by contrast to the ordinary buildings around it. It also prevented visitors from seeing the whole facade until they were very close, close enough that it towered up terrifically before them. Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.
Sitte thought that cities should move in the opposite direction. The Votive Church in Vienna was built in the 1870s on what Sitte described as a ‘desolate monster plaza’ that was ‘intolerably exposed to high wind, inclement weather, heat and dust, as well as to the din of the streets, and the incessant clanging of trams.’ The church does indeed have an awkward and lonely feeling. Sitte thought that the architecture of the building was actually very good, and that the defects in its effect were entirely the fault of its location. He proposed building up regular urban fabric on most of the ‘monster plaza’, defining three small squares with well-framed views onto the church. Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.
Another way to understand this contrast is to look at whole cities planned on Sittesque and anti-Sittesque principles. The pictures below show Padua and Washington DC. It is as though a figure-ground switch has taken place: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings. Monumental buildings in Washington sit alone on their city blocks, untouched by vernacular fabric. Monumental buildings in Padua constantly link up with vernacular fabric to shape small, sheltered spaces from which they can be properly enjoyed.
The rise, fall, and rise of Camillo Sitte
The Art of Building Cities was an immediate success, landing, in the words of Sitte’s English translator Charles T Stewart, ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’. Within a year of publication it had prompted the redrawing of urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and Sitte was being approached by town officials seeking his advice on their own plans. By Sitte’s death in 1903, advocates of his ideas were to be found in prestigious positions in cities including Munich, Berlin, and Vienna, either teaching or as official city architects.
Two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate the effect of Sittesque ideas on urban planning. In the nineteenth century, Helsinki followed a neoclassical grid plan, with straight streets meeting at right angles. In the early twentieth century, it switched dramatically to a Sittesque approach, introducing curving streets, turbine squares, T-junctions, and asymmetrical spaces. The resulting neighborhood is full of pleasing, characterful spaces and unexpected ‘old town’ effects, even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor.
But Sitte’s influence was curiously short-lived. In the decades following Sitte’s death in 1903, European urban design came to be dominated by the modernist movement. Everything that Sitte hated about nineteenth-century planning was vastly amplified in modernism. With honorable exception, the modernists treated public space as merely whatever was left over after the buildings had been placed, and had no sympathy with Sitte’s approach of treating spaces as primary and shaping the buildings around them. Instead of lining the edge of a city block with buildings (a ‘perimeter block’) they preferred to orient all blocks in the same direction (‘parallel blocks’), often with a seemingly arbitrary angle to the street. Sitte had decried the gridiron blocks of the nineteenth century for the weakly defined spaces they created. But by twentieth-century standards, the straight ‘corridor streets’ of the nineteenth century look comparatively Sittesque.
Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.
Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘New Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. But the Sittesque revival goes far beyond this. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.
Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.
Phoebe Arslanagic-Little is a writer and policy researcher.
Samuel Hughes is an editor at Works in Progress.

Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop
Unknown

2026-11-24
16:18:12 UTC
01:18:12 KST

Jensen Huang is partying it up in Ibiza. In a video with nearly 6 million views on Instagram, the former CEO of Nvidia is dancing in a crowded club, champagne glass in hand, still wearing his signature black leather jacket. Suddenly, from behind him, Alice Huang — the Chinese technology executive and suspected spy he had an affair with, sparking congressional investigations and his resignation from the chipmaking company he cofounded — appears. She puts her hand on his shoulder and he wraps his arm around her waist as they begin dancing together. The video’s caption reads “Honey Trap Final Boss. #inthemoodforlove.”
Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop
Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop
Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
Of course, it’s AI-generated. This Instagram Reel is one of hundreds of AI deepfakes featuring Huang, his wife Lori, Alice, and sometimes Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell (the second of three reported affair partners). In this case, Huang is being swapped into an existing meme called “Ibiza Final Boss.” The original video featured a British construction worker with a bowl cut dancing in exactly the same way, minus a woman sidling up to him. Other viral AI hits include Huang in a scene from The Office, Huang in the music video for George Michael’s “Careless Whisper,” and Huang as the former Astronomer CEO who got caught in an affair with one of his employees by the jumbotron at a Coldplay concert last summer. Even the rapper 50 Cent posted an AI edit of his “P.I.M.P.” music video, now featuring Huang with some flashy silver accessories.
Unlike deepfake pornography or election disinformation, these AI videos aren’t necessarily intended to harm or mislead people. They’re memes making fun of Huang’s cheating scandal and its global implications, created with AI technology that in many cases relies heavily on Nvidia’s tech stack: video diffusion models running on the Nvidia GPUs that power much of the modern generative AI industry. “It’s ironic that without Nvidia generating millions of these AI memes ... would not be possible,” reads one of the top comments on the Ibiza deepfake. “In some sense, Jensen is making Nvidia richer by his own scandal.” The comment was punctuated by multiple cry-laughing emoji.
As it turns out, Huang may benefit, too. On Monday, the Nvidia board announced he was reinstated as president, CEO, and board director following “a series of discussions and meetings” and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” Nvidia’s stock has since surged, and new AI Huang memes cast him in a victorious light. One variation swaps him into a scene from The Wolf of Wall Street, announcing “I’m not leaving” to a crowd of cheering men that has been edited to include AI versions of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerberg.
While the saga continues, many social media users are finding the humor in these Huang deepfakes, and their creators are churning out variations to meet the sudden demand. The Instagram account behind the Ibiza one has made three Huang deepfakes so far, all remakes of the same scene. Another version features Powell dancing with him, and the third one shows a sea of young women in bikini tops and shorts surrounding Huang, who lifts his champagne up in celebration. Each has accrued millions of views.
“His story has just come at the best time for ai creators and a terrible time for him,” wrote the account behind the Ibiza videos in a direct message to The Verge. “Everyone was doing him. Most I’ve seen anyone AI-ed.”
This deepfake creator identified himself as a 40-year-old man from Melbourne, Australia, but wouldn’t share his real name. He says he has spent “thousands” on AI video generation, using models like TikTok developer ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 and Alibaba’s Wan 3. These, along with other AI tools like Google’s Nano Banana, help power the ecosystem of deepfakes.
He said his Instagram page has been going “super viral” in the past two weeks, thanks to the Ibiza meme format. He has nearly 100 million views on various iterations of it featuring different celebrities. The Huang ones are among the most popular, alongside versions featuring Elizabeth Holmes and Amanda Seyfried playing her in the hit Nathan Fielder documentary You Can See Everything.
“I wanted to elevate the content and know that putting what is happening in the news ... would get traction,” he wrote. “Always wanted to be a filmmaker but this technology is beyond whatever I imagined was possible.”
As generative AI has taken hold of the internet in recent years, a lot of the resulting viral content has been disparaged as “AI slop.” Hollywood productions, mainstream artists, and even local businesses have been maligned for using (or appearing to use) AI in their advertisements and final cuts. Video trends like putting sexy AI fruit characters in Love Island parodies racked up millions of views online but failed to deliver any real cultural momentum. The ubiquity of the Huang deepfakes and the relative lack of blowback from AI critics may indicate that the future of AI-generated content is similar to the rest of meme culture: If the topic’s trending, people will engage with something, even if it’s following the same formula as the slop. That an AI tech titan’s own indiscretions are inspiring this latest evolution in deepfakes is just the sardonic cherry on top.
“It’s not that we’re inundated in deepfakes of Trump being like ‘Nuclear war tomorrow,’ like the way it was framed as the big problem,” says misinformation researcher Abbie Richards. “Instead, it just feels like there is so much slop to push through to have any grounding in reality.”
The AI memes of Huang and other public figures don’t feel as sinister as other forms of AI disinformation and misinformation, mainly because of how goofy they are. It’s hard to imagine anyone falling for a “Gangnam Style” parody or any serious implications if they did. But these deepfakes are still eerily realistic, as one comment on the Seyfried Ibiza variation pointed out: “All jokes aside, is anyone else finding it increasingly alarming that AI is capable of this?”
Even the creator behind the Ibiza AI videos thinks “someone will try and clamp down because it’s getting outta control.” But in the meantime, he’s looking for ways to monetize his newfound virality. Despite his significant financial outlay, he says he hasn’t made any money yet, besides getting “gifted $3 on a reel once.”
While Instagram has started to invite some creators to earn direct payouts from views on their Reels, the account behind the AI “Careless Whisper” parody featuring Huang told The Verge that “the way to earn is through creating content for clients and companies after gaining attention on social media.” This AI creator, who declined to share any identifying information, wrote in a direct message that they receive dozens of requests from new and returning clients for AI commissions every time they go viral, “which is quite often.” In addition to Huang deepfakes, some of their most viral AI edits feature Tobey Maguire’s Spider-Man as a rapper.
The Ibiza AI meme creator has worked with one celebrity brand so far, belonging to the Irish mixed martial artist Conor McGregor. Four months ago, McGregor launched an energy drink called MAC Energy, and the company requested an AI Ibiza meme showing McGregor dancing with a can of it. The creator complied, and the post exists as a collaboration between the two Instagram pages, but it isn’t labeled as an advertisement and he says he didn’t ask for any money in return.
“I just did it because it was a good opportunity for my page,” he says.
It seems like the entity that stands to reap the biggest reward from viral Huang deepfakes is Instagram itself and the other social media sites where creators are posting them. And these humorous AI edits are technically allowed on Meta platforms, as long as creators disclose that they’re AI-generated. Meta didn’t respond to a request for comment by publication time.
But there are other considerations besides profitability. Many of these AI memes hinge on sexist portrayals and racist stereotypes as the joke. Asian American women in Silicon Valley have reported an uptick in microaggressions revolving around “honeypot” and “Chinese spy” allegations. And when it comes to Powell and the other Nvidia employee who Huang reportedly had a relationship with, the workplace power dynamic at play has faded into the background of mockery.
The more troubling dynamics of Huang’s affairs have faded into the background of mockery
“Even though we know that he was wielding his power to have inappropriate relationships with his subordinates and his employees, it’s still like ‘LOL, let’s make an AI deepfake of him at the office,’” says Josh Lora, a writer and creator who has a popular TikTok series about the role of cheating scandals in American culture. “Why aren’t we having a real conversation about the effects of this on women, the effects of this workplace on women, especially 10 years after #MeToo?”
The apparent lack of interest from major social media companies to stem the flow of this kind of disparaging AI content isn’t surprising to misinformation expert Richards, even as some tech CEOs, like Elon Musk, called for Huang’s reinstatement and cast doubt on the reporting against him. If Huang memes are truly in vogue, that may be worth more to the AI industry than his dignity.
“I think that they are invested in the widespread adoption of AI,” she says. “So anything with AI going viral and appearing to be popular and liked by the public probably, in their mind, benefits them.”
With Huang back as CEO, the message couldn’t be clearer: For him, the consequences of his affairs were temporary, including whatever humiliation stemmed from the AI memes. Ultimately, all any of it meant was more power for Nvidia and more power for Jensen Huang.

Tidal bans AI-generated music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:12:38 UTC
01:12:38 KST

The music streaming service Tidal said Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated starting next month, a move its leader believes “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”
The service will remove the AI tracks starting Dec. 9, making Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely. It comes nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted and ban AI songs that were associated with “fraudulent activity,” a category that includes songs impersonating established artists and efforts to “deceive listeners.”
“But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” wrote Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, in an X thread on Tuesday. “We’ll begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from our catalog, and you’ll see them completely gone by the beginning of the year.”
Andersen said that 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. The move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks, he added, and have it reject between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day.
“We encourage our peers to follow suit,” he wrote.
The move comes as competitors such as Spotify and Apple Music continue to test approaches to combat the rise of AI-generated tracks proliferating on their platforms, many of which the services have labeled some version of “slop” or “spam.” Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform, while Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an “AI Persona.”
Spotify said in a blog post last month it also removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users’ recommendations this year, which came after it removed 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. The revelation came among a number of updates regarding Spotify’s efforts to combat AI spam.
“This work isn’t finished,” Spotify added. “AI moves fast, and bad actors adapt just as fast. But as AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more. Our job is to make Spotify the place they find it.”

Show HN: Mason – a lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:11:52 UTC
01:11:52 KST

A lightweight drop-in replacement for your Postgres read replica.
Same SQL, same answers. But extremely fast for analytical queries.
AWS m7g.xlarge · 4 vCPU · 16 GiB RAM · EBS gp3
Why Mason
- Lightweight: Mason is a single Node.js process you can run anywhere. It keeps all its config and your synced data locally in the folder you run it in.
- Fast: Mason syncs your Postgres data into DuckDB's columnar engine, and rewrites your Postgres queries on the fly into the form DuckDB runs fastest.
- Postgres: Mason is built from the ground up to match Postgres's syntax and behavior (not DuckDB's), so you can point your existing Postgres queries at it with confidence.
- Read replica: You choose which tables and columns to sync from your Postgres database, and how each stays in sync: on demand, by polling or by logical replication.
- Built for AI agents: Add a user per agent, with role-based access control (RBAC) that limits the tables, columns and rows each one can read. Every query is logged with who ran it, the SQL they sent, how long it took and, if it was refused, how to fix it. Mason also has MCP support built in.
Try it out in minutes, run it anywhere
$ npm i -g @mason-data/cli
$ cd my-app
# tell Mason which Postgres database to sync from
$ mason init 'postgres://me:secret@db.example.com:5432/my_db'
# choose the tables to sync
$ mason add orders customers
# start Mason locally and wait for the first sync to finish
$ mason start && mason wait
# get a connection URL for your favorite Postgres client
$ mason user add me
# get results fast
$ psql "postgres://me:<password>@localhost:5433/mason" -c "SELECT country, sum(amount) FROM orders JOIN customers ON customers.id = customer_id GROUP BY country"
# or give it to your coding agent
$ claude mcp add mason --env MASON_URL="postgres://me:<password>@localhost:5433/mason" -- mason mcp
# done? stop Mason and delete its synced copy of your data
$ mason stop && mason destroy
Where Mason is fast, and where it isn't
Fast
Queries that read lots of rows, like counts, sums and group-bys over big tables. The kind dashboards, reports and AI agents run.
Not fast
Queries that fetch a few rows and many columns, like looking up one order by its ID. Mason is fastest when you're querying a lot of rows across a few columns.
From a cold start: each engine restarted and the page cache dropped before every run. 1 or 10 clients send the query at the same moment, and the time is until every client has its answer, the median of 3 runs. Actual results will vary, depending on the size and distribution of your data.
How it was measuredAWS m7g.xlarge · 4 vCPU · 16 GiB RAM · EBS gp3
Features
- Role-based access control: Mason gives each tool, AI agent or customer its own login, and its role decides which tables and columns it can read. You can add, disable or remove a user at any time, and the change takes effect immediately.
- Row-level security: You can limit each user to its own rows, such as the rows for one customer. Mason applies the same limit to related tables by following their foreign keys.
- Generated tables: These are like materialized views, but Mason keeps them up to date for you. They put no extra load on your database.
- MCP: Mason has its own MCP server, so AI agents like Claude Code and ChatGPT can look at your tables and run queries. Each agent can only see what its role allows.
- Monitoring: Mason works with the monitoring tools you already use. Prometheus and Grafana can read its metrics at /metrics, and uptime checks, Kubernetes and ECS can check its health at /healthz. It writes its logs to stdout, so Datadog or CloudWatch can collect them. You can also look back at every query, every sync event and how busy Mason has been, with mason logs and mason usage.
- IP allowlists and TLS: You can limit each user to the IP addresses it connects from. Mason can also encrypt every connection, with your own certificate or with one it makes for you.
- Web UI: Run mason ui to open a web page where you can add tables and users. The page also shows you queries, usage and sync events as they happen.

Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:10:00 UTC
01:10:00 KST

The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.
“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”
It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.
That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.
“Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”
Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.
G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.
The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.
“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”
In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.
Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.
“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.
It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.
Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see

Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

Millions of bitcoin are probably lost for good. Almost none can be proved gone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:01:24 UTC
01:01:24 KST

Millions of bitcoin are probably lost for good. Almost none can be proved gone
Estimates put the lost coins at 2.8 to 3.8 million. Only a sliver can be shown to be gone; the rest is a landfill, a password and a guess.
About 20.1 million bitcoin have been mined so far. A good share of them will probably never move again.
In 2017 the analytics firm Chainalysis estimated that between 2.78 million and 3.79 million BTC were already lost, Fortune reported. That was 17% to 23% of the coins mined at the time.
It is still the figure most reports quote, and it rests on assumptions. A coin that hasn't moved in ten years might be lost, or its owner might just be patient. The blockchain can't tell the difference.
The coins nobody has touched since 2010
The biggest pile of unmoved bitcoin is also the oldest. In 2013 the researcher Sergio Demian Lerner spotted a pattern in the earliest blocks that points to a single miner, since nicknamed "Patoshi".
He estimates that miner earned about 1.1 million BTC, and almost none of it has ever been spent, Cointelegraph reports. Many people assume the miner was Bitcoin's creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. Lerner himself says that can't be proved. Whether those coins count as lost depends on who is counting. That one choice moves the estimate by about a million.
A hard drive in Newport
In 2013 James Howells threw out a hard drive holding the keys to 8,000 BTC. It ended up in a landfill run by Newport City Council in Wales, according to Wikipedia's account of the case.
For more than a decade he asked to dig for it. The council refused, the High Court dismissed his claim in January 2025, and the Court of Appeal refused to let it go further that March. The drive is still in the ground.
Eight wrong guesses
Stefan Thomas, a programmer, was paid 7,002 BTC in 2011 for making an explainer video about bitcoin. He kept the keys on an encrypted IronKey drive and lost the paper with its password.
The drive allows ten tries before it encrypts its contents for good. He had used eight, Cointelegraph reported in 2021, and later reports still describe him as having two left.
The vault that wasn't
Some "lost keys" stories turn out to be something else. When Gerald Cotten, the founder of the Canadian exchange QuadrigaCX, died in December 2018, the exchange said its customers' crypto sat in cold wallets only he could open.
A 2020 staff review by the Ontario Securities Commission found otherwise. It said most of the shortfall came from fraud by Cotten, rejected the idea that the money was locked in cold wallets nobody could open, and put clients' losses at at least C$169 million.
Read more: Was FTX a Ponzi scheme from the beginning?
Burned on purpose
Some bitcoin is lost on purpose. Coins sent to an address like 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE can never be spent, because nobody holds a key for it. People use addresses like this to "burn" coins in public.
Even the first block has some. The 50 BTC reward in the genesis block can't be spent because of a quirk in Bitcoin's original code, according to the Bitcoin Wiki. Coins like these are the only ones anyone can prove are gone, and they are a tiny share of the total.
A supply nobody can count exactly
Bitcoin's 21 million cap is fixed in its code. Supply passed 20 million in March 2026, The Block reported, and the last coins will be issued over the next century or so. Lost coins don't change those numbers. They still count as supply, in wallets that will never sign another transaction.
Mt. Gox shows how blurry the line can be. About 850,000 BTC went missing there in 2014, and about 200,000 turned up in an old wallet a month later. Its creditors are still being paid, twelve years on.
So "lost bitcoin" is mostly an estimate, with a few cases that are certain. Everything else sits somewhere between a landfill and a wallet whose owner is just very patient.
Read more: Is CeFi less secure than DeFi?
Frequently asked questions
How many bitcoins are lost?
Nobody knows exactly. The most quoted figure is a 2017 Chainalysis estimate of 2.78 million to 3.79 million BTC, which was 17% to 23% of the coins mined at the time. It treats long-unmoved coins as probably lost, so it is an estimate, not a count.
Can lost bitcoin be recovered?
Only by someone who has, or finds, the private key. There is no central party that can reissue or reverse coins. Coins sent to a burn address, or the genesis block reward, can't be spent by anyone.
Are Satoshi Nakamoto's coins lost?
Nobody knows. About 1.1 million BTC mined in 2009 and 2010 is attributed to one early miner, often assumed to be Satoshi, and almost none of it has moved. The attribution can't be proved, and unmoved coins are not necessarily lost.
Do lost coins reduce bitcoin's 21 million cap?
No. The cap and the issuance schedule are fixed in the code, and lost coins still count in supply figures. They simply can't move, so fewer coins are usable than the supply number suggests.
What is a bitcoin burn address?
An address that nobody holds a private key for, often a readable "vanity" string such as 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE. Coins sent there are visible on the blockchain but can never be spent again.

Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the gap with Nvidia in the AI chip race

Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”
